<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<p id="p3.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:144%;">Generalized Weyl Solutions</span></p>
<p id="p3.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">Roberto Emparan<sup id="p3.2.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p3.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">a,</span></sup><span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
          Also at Departamento de Física
Teórica, Universidad del País Vasco, E-48080, Bilbao, Spain.</span></span></span>
and
Harvey S. Reall<sup id="p3.2.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p3.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">b</span></sup></p>
<p id="p3.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><sup id="p3.3.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p3.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">a</span></sup><span id="p3.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Theory Division, CERN
<br class="ltx_break">CH-1211 Geneva 23, Switzerland
<br class="ltx_break"></span></p>
<p id="p3.4" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><sup id="p3.4.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p3.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">b</span></sup><span id="p3.4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Physics Department, Queen Mary College
<br class="ltx_break">Mile End Road, London E1 4NS, United Kingdom
<br class="ltx_break"></span></p>
</div>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">It was shown by Weyl that the general static axisymmetric solution of
the vacuum Einstein equations in four dimensions is given in terms of a
single axisymmetric solution of the Laplace equation in
three-dimensional flat space. Weyl’s construction is generalized here to
arbitrary dimension <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D\geq 4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D\geq 4</annotation></semantics></math>. The general solution of the
<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional vacuum Einstein equations that admits <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-2</annotation></semantics></math> orthogonal
commuting non-null Killing vector fields is given either in terms of
<math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-3</annotation></semantics></math> independent axisymmetric solutions of Laplace’s equation in
three-dimensional flat space or by <math id="abstract1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-4</annotation></semantics></math> independent solutions of
Laplace’s equation in two-dimensional flat space. Explicit examples of
new solutions are given. These include a five-dimensional asymptotically
flat “black ring” with an event horizon of topology <math id="abstract1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}\times S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}\times S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>
held in equilibrium by a conical singularity in the form of a disc.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Exact solutions play an important role in General Relativity.
Examining properties of exact solutions has led to deep insights into
the nature of spacetime that would have been hard to arrive at by
other means. For example, much of the progress made in understanding
properties of black holes in the 60’s and 70’s relied on the existence
of the Kerr-Newman solution. The Standard Model of cosmology is built
on Friedman-Robertson-Walker solutions. Examining properties of
Bianchi cosmologies has led to insight into how inflation dissipates
anisotropy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Much effort has been devoted to developing techniques for finding exact
solutions in four dimensions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>. One of the
earliest results in this direction was obtained by Weyl <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>,
who found the general static axisymmetric solution of the vacuum
Einstein equations:</p>
<table id="S1.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ds^{2}=-e^{2U}dt^{2}+e^{-2U}\left(e^{2\gamma}(dr^{2}+dz^{2})+r^{2}d\phi^{2}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ds^{2}=-e^{2U}dt^{2}+e^{-2U}\left(e^{2\gamma}(dr^{2}+dz^{2})+r^{2}d\phi^{2}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1.1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U(r,z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U(r,z)</annotation></semantics></math> is an arbitrary axisymmetric solution of Laplace’s
equation in a three-dimensional <span id="S1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">flat</span> space with metric</p>
<table id="S1.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ds^{2}=dr^{2}+r^{2}d\phi^{2}+dz^{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ds^{2}=dr^{2}+r^{2}d\phi^{2}+dz^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1.2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">and <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> satisfies</p>
<table id="S1.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial\gamma}{\partial r}=r\left[\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial r}\right)^{2}-\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial z}\right)^{2}\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial\gamma}{\partial r}=r\left[\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial r}\right)^{2}-\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial z}\right)^{2}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1.3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<table id="S1.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial\gamma}{\partial z}=2r\frac{\partial U}{\partial r}\frac{\partial U}{\partial z}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial\gamma}{\partial z}=2r\frac{\partial U}{\partial r}\frac{\partial U}{\partial z}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1.4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.p2.4" class="ltx_p">The solution of these equations is given by a line integral. Since <math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math>
is harmonic, it can be regarded as a Newtonian potential produced by
certain (axisymmetric) sources. For example, the Schwarzschild
solution corresponds to taking the source for <math id="S1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math> to be a thin rod on
the <math id="S1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>-axis with mass <math id="S1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/2</annotation></semantics></math> per unit length.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Nowadays, interest in solutions of General Relativity is no longer
restricted to four dimensions. Many interesting solutions of higher
dimensional supergravity theories have been found. In spite of this,
there are basic questions concerning the nature of gravity in higher
dimensions that remain unanswered. In four dimensions, it can be proved
that each connected component of the event horizon of an asymptotically
flat spacetime satisfying the dominant energy condition has topology
<math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>. The proof relies on the Gauss-Bonnet theorem
applied to a constant time slice through the horizon, and is therefore
invalid in higher dimensions. A different approach to rule out
non-spherical topologies is based on the notion of ‘topological
censorship’ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>. However, this argument is typically
phrased in terms of non-contractible loops that begin and end at
infinity, and which would thread through a toroidal horizon. In higher
dimensions, one can always unlink two loops by moving them apart in a
fourth spatial direction. This suggests that it might be possible for
the event horizon to have non-spherical topology in higher dimensions.
Indeed, in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, it was argued that the horizon of a
time-symmetric black hole in five dimensions must have topology given
by a connected sum of <math id="S1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}\times S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}\times S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> terms, subject to the
weak energy condition. Nevertheless, no example of an asymptotically
flat solution with a non-spherical event horizon has ever been
found<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
          A solution with a regular, though degenerate, horizon
of topology <math id="footnote2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}\times S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}\times S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> has been found in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>.
Although not asymptotically flat, this solution has a spacelike
infinity of topology <math id="footnote2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, which distinguishes it from examples in
which horizons of non-spherical topology are constructed by taking
spacelike infinity to have non-spherical topology.</span></span></span>. One aim of the
present paper is to provide an example of such a spacetime.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We will, for simplicity, consider only the vacuum Einstein equations. A
lot of work has been devoted to finding exact solutions of these
equations in dimensions <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D&gt;4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D&gt;4</annotation></semantics></math>. Most of this work has looked for
solutions with a Kaluza-Klein (KK) interpretation, i.e., solutions with
a Killing vector field along which one can perform dimensional
reduction to get a sensible lower dimensional spacetime. For example,
KK black hole solutions were discussed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> and a KK
monopole solution was presented in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>. KK
generalizations of the C-metric <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> and Ernst metric
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> were presented in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>. Other axially
symmetric solutions in KK theory have been discussed in
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Less work has been devoted to finding solutions of the <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional
vacuum Einstein equations that do <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">not</span> admit a KK interpretation,
either because they do not admit an appropriate Killing vector field
along which KK reduction can be performed, or because the reduced
spacetime has pathological features. Examples of such spacetimes are
provided by higher dimensional versions of the Schwarzschild and Kerr
black holes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>. When Wick rotated, these
solutions <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">do</span> admit KK interpretations as describing instabilities
of the KK vacuum <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> or of KK magnetic fields
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>, but their most natural interpretation is
certainly as higher dimensional black holes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The purpose of the present paper is to obtain and analyze the higher
dimensional analogues of Weyl’s class of solutions. Depending on which
feature of Weyl’s class one focuses on, there are several directions in
which one can try to extend it to higher dimensions. One possibility is
to seek the class of <math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional solutions that are static and
axisymmetric, in the sense that they admit an isometry group <math id="S1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf R}\times O(D-2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐑</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf R}\times O(D-2)</annotation></semantics></math> (with <math id="S1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐑</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf R}</annotation></semantics></math> being time translations). However, this
has been tried before <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> without success. Instead, observe
that Weyl’s solutions can be characterized as having two orthogonal
commuting Killing vector fields. Hence an alternative way to generalize
Weyl’s solutions to higher dimensions is to find all solutions of the
vacuum Einstein equations that admit <math id="S1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-2</annotation></semantics></math> orthogonal commuting Killing
vector fields. This is done in section <a href="#S2" title="2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> of this paper.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">As in four dimensions, the higher-dimensional Weyl class of solutions is
parametrized in terms of axisymmetric harmonic functions in an auxiliary
flat space. Actually, there are <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">two</span> classes of Weyl solutions in
higher dimensions. The first, and the most interesting one, is
parametrized in terms of <math id="S1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-3</annotation></semantics></math> harmonic functions in three-dimensional
flat space, and is the natural analogue of the <math id="S1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> Weyl solutions
discussed above. The second class of solutions (discussed in Appendix
<a href="#A2" title="Appendix B The special Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>) is parametrized in terms of <math id="S1.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-4</annotation></semantics></math> harmonic
functions in <span id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">two</span>-dimensional flat space, and therefore has no
<math id="S1.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> analogue.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Although Weyl’s construction in <math id="S1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> describes an infinite class of
solutions, most of them are unphysical in the sense that they are not
asymptotically flat, or have naked curvature singularities on the axis
of symmetry<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
            
            
          E.g., a spherically symmetric point source for <math id="footnote3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math>
results in a singular, <span id="footnote3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">non-spherical</span> Chazy-Curzon particle.</span></span></span>. The
same is true for <math id="S1.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D&gt;4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D&gt;4</annotation></semantics></math>. In order to select candidate Weyl solutions
that might be of physical importance, recall that for <math id="S1.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math>, the
harmonic function <math id="S1.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math> can be regarded as a Newtonian potential produced
by an axisymmetric source. It turns out that the most interesting <math id="S1.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math>
Weyl solutions all have sources of the same form, namely thin
rods on the axis of symmetry. In section <a href="#S3" title="3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, known <math id="S1.p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D&gt;4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D&gt;4</annotation></semantics></math>
Weyl solutions of physical importance are analyzed. Their harmonic
functions also always correspond to thin rods on the axis of symmetry
in the auxiliary three-dimensional flat space.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">A natural classification scheme for such solutions is presented in
section <a href="#S4" title="4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. In this scheme, the ‘zeroth’ class consists
simply of flat space. The first non-trivial class contains just the
<math id="S1.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math> Schwarzschild solutions (the <math id="S1.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D&gt;5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D&gt;5</annotation></semantics></math> Schwarzschild
solutions do not admit <math id="S1.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-2</annotation></semantics></math> commuting Killing vector fields and are
therefore not Weyl solutions), and their Wick rotations. These Wick
rotations describe objects known as ‘KK bubbles’. If one considers the
Euclideanized <math id="S1.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> Schwarzschild solution, then the solution looks
asymptotically like <math id="S1.p9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf R}^{3}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐑</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf R}^{3}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, the <math id="S1.p9.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponding to
Euclidean time, which is periodically identified and can be regarded as
a KK compactified dimension. However, the actual topology of the
solution is <math id="S1.p9.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf R}^{2}\times S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐑</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf R}^{2}\times S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. The size of the two-spheres at
constant radius decreases from infinity to a minimum non-zero value at
the location of the Euclidean horizon, where a non-contractible <math id="S1.p9.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>
lies. At this point, the KK circles smoothly round off and space cannot
be continued past this radius. By adding a flat Lorentzian time
direction one obtains a solution to <math id="S1.p9.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math> KK theory where the
non-contractible sphere is a static ‘bubble of nothing’. It is known to
be unstable <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>. A related solution is obtained by Wick
rotating both the time and one of the ignorable angular coordinates of
the five-dimensional Schwarzschild solution. The Wick-rotated angle then
becomes a boost coordinate and the solution describes a bubble
exponentially expanding in the five-dimensional KK vacuum
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>. Its fully Euclideanized version is an instanton
mediating the decay of the KK vacuum <math id="S1.p9.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{1,3}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{1,3}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">The second class of Weyl solutions contains the <math id="S1.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> C-metric as well
as three new solutions. The most interesting of these is a Wick
rotated version of a <math id="S1.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math> metric discussed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, and
can also be related to the KK C-metric of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>. It is a
static, asymptotically flat solution with an event horizon of topology
<math id="S1.p10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}\times S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}\times S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., it is a <span id="S1.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">black ring</span>.
This is the first example of an
asymptotically flat solution of the vacuum Einstein equations that has
an event horizon of non-spherical topology. The solution is not
entirely satisfactory since it has a conical singularity, but it will
be shown in a separate publication that this singularity can be
eliminated if the ring rotates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p11.1" class="ltx_p">The two other new solutions in the same class as the black ring and the
C-metric both describe superpositions of black objects with static KK
bubbles. These solutions are entirely regular outside an event horizon.
The first is a <math id="S1.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math> solution describing a black hole sitting in the
throat of a static KK bubble. The second is a <math id="S1.p11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=6</annotation></semantics></math> solution describing
a loop of black string with horizon topology <math id="S1.p11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> sitting
in the throat of a static KK bubble. These solutions asymptote to,
respectively, the KK vacua <math id="S1.p11.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{1,3}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{1,3}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.p11.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{1,4}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{1,4}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Both are expected to be unstable. In fact, the evolution of the
instability of the former solution can be obtained by a Wick rotation
of the black ring. If these solutions are Euclideanized then they give
new non-singular instantons for the decay of the <math id="S1.p11.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> compactified KK
vacuum in <math id="S1.p11.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.p11.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=6</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p12.1" class="ltx_p">Many of the solutions we describe are naturally interpreted in terms of
KK compactification along the orbits of one or several of the Killing
vector fields. When there is more than one Killing vector field with
closed orbits, one can often dimensionally reduce along different
linear combinations of them. Physically distinct reduced spacetimes can
therefore arise from the same higher dimensional spacetime. A good
example is the KK C-metric and the KK Ernst solution, which are locally
isometric in five dimensions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>. With this in mind,
different KK reductions of the new solutions found in this paper are
briefly discussed in section <a href="#S4.SS8" title="4.8 Different KK reductions ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.8</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p13.1" class="ltx_p">Multi-black hole configurations can be readily constructed within Weyl’s
class, and are briefly discussed in section <a href="#S4.SS9" title="4.9 Multi-black hole configurations ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.9</span></a>.
Finally, Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Concluding remarks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> contains the conclusions of this
work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Generalized Weyl solutions</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Integrable submanifolds</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The first step in generalizing Weyl’s construction to more than four
dimensions is to find a convenient coordinate chart for the general
<math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional line element admitting <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-2</annotation></semantics></math> commuting Killing vector
fields (orthogonality of these vector fields will not be assumed yet).
This is a simple generalization of what is done in four dimensions (see
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> for a review). It will be assumed that the metric is
Riemannian or Lorentzian. Let <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the Killing vector
fields, <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\leq i\leq D-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\leq i\leq D-2</annotation></semantics></math>. Since these commute, it is possible to choose
coordinates <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x^{i},y^{1},y^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x^{i},y^{1},y^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(i)}=\partial/\partial x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mo rspace="0.055em">/</mo><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}=\partial/\partial x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> with the metric coefficients depending only on <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The next step is to show that one can choose the coordinates <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> to span two-dimensional surfaces orthogonal to all of the
<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math>. In order to do this, one has to show that the
two-dimensional subspaces of the tangent space orthogonal to all of the
vectors <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> are integrable, i.e., tangent to two-dimensional
surfaces. Sufficient conditions for integrability are supplied by the
following theorem:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem</span>. Let <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\leq i\leq D-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\leq i\leq D-2</annotation></semantics></math> be commuting Killing
vector fields such that for each <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, (a) <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\xi_{(1)}^{[\mu_{1}}\xi_{(2)}^{\mu_{2}}\ldots\xi_{(D-2)}^{\mu_{D-2}}\nabla^{\nu}\xi_{(i)}^{\rho]}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ξ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>μ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msup><mi>ξ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mi>ξ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></msup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>ν</mi></msup><mi>ξ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(1)}^{[\mu_{1}}\xi_{(2)}^{\mu_{2}}\ldots\xi_{(D-2)}^{\mu_{D-2}}\nabla^{\nu}\xi_{(i)}^{\rho]}</annotation></semantics></math>
vanishes at at least one point of the spacetime (not necessarily the
same point for every <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>), and
(b) <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\xi_{(i)}^{\nu}R_{\nu}^{[\rho}\xi_{(1)}^{\mu_{1}}\xi_{(2)}^{\mu_{2}}\ldots\xi_{(D-2)}^{\mu_{D-2}]}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ξ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>ν</mi></msup><mi>R</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>ν</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow></msup><mi>ξ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msup><mi>ξ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mi>ξ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>μ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}^{\nu}R_{\nu}^{[\rho}\xi_{(1)}^{\mu_{1}}\xi_{(2)}^{\mu_{2}}\ldots\xi_{(D-2)}^{\mu_{D-2}]}=0</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then the two planes orthogonal to the <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> are integrable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The proof of this theorem is a straightforward generalization of the
corresponding theorem in four dimensions, as given in
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>. In this paper, only
vacuum solutions of the Einstein equations will be considered so
condition (b) is trivially satisfied. Condition (a) is less obvious;
in four dimensions it is usually assumed that one of the Killing
vector fields is an angular coordinate corresponding to rotations
about an axis of symmetry, and must therefore vanish on this axis,
which ensures that condition (a) is obeyed. The same assumption can be
used to motivate condition (a) in the higher dimensional case. Of
course, this is not the only way in which condition (a) can be
satisfied, so this theorem has wider applicability than just metrics
with an axis of rotational symmetry.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">If the conditions of this theorem are met then the coordinates <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>
and <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> can be chosen in one of the orthogonal surfaces and then
extended along the integral curves of the Killing vector fields<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
              
              
            It is
necessary to assume that the <math id="footnote4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> are non-null at this point.</span></span></span>.
In this coordinate system, the vectors <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial/\partial y^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mo rspace="0.055em">/</mo><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial/\partial y^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are
orthogonal to <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial/\partial x^{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mo rspace="0.055em">/</mo><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial/\partial x^{j}</annotation></semantics></math>. If it is further assumed that
the Killing vector fields are orthogonal to each other
then the metric must take the form</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ds^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{D-2}\epsilon_{i}e^{2U_{i}}(dx^{i})^{2}+g_{ab}dy^{a}dy^{b}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>a</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ds^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{D-2}\epsilon_{i}e^{2U_{i}}(dx^{i})^{2}+g_{ab}dy^{a}dy^{b},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2.1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> take the values <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1,2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1,2</annotation></semantics></math>, the metric coefficients are
independent of <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{i}=\pm 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{i}=\pm 1</annotation></semantics></math> according to whether
<math id="S2.SS1.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> is spacelike or timelike.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The final step is to use the freedom to perform coordinate
transformations on <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y^{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>a</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y^{a}</annotation></semantics></math>. Locally it is always possible to choose
coordinates such that</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{ab}dy^{a}dy^{b}=e^{2C}dZd\bar{Z}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>a</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mi>b</mi></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{ab}dy^{a}dy^{b}=e^{2C}dZd\bar{Z},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2.2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p6.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> are complex conjugate coordinates if the
transverse space is spacelike, and independent real coordinates if it is
timelike.<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
              
              
            The term “Weyl solution” is usually reserved for
static solutions (i.e. a spacelike transverse space)
but we adopt a more general usage here.</span></span></span> The function
<math id="S2.SS1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> is independent of <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Solving the Einstein equations</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have shown that any <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional metric that admits <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-2</annotation></semantics></math>
orthogonal commuting Killing vector fields can be written locally in
the form</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ds^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{D-2}\epsilon_{i}e^{2U_{i}}(dx^{i})^{2}+e^{2C}dZd\bar{Z}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ds^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{D-2}\epsilon_{i}e^{2U_{i}}(dx^{i})^{2}+e^{2C}dZd\bar{Z},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2.3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> are functions of <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> only, and
<math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{i}=\pm 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{i}=\pm 1</annotation></semantics></math>. The summation convention will not be used for
indices <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i,j,\ldots" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i,j,\ldots</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The components of the curvature tensors of this line element are
calculated in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Curvature components" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>. The vacuum Einstein
equations read <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mu\nu}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ν</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mu\nu}=0</annotation></semantics></math>. The <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ij" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ij</annotation></semantics></math> component gives</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial_{Z}\left[\exp\left(\sum_{j}U_{j}\right)\partial_{\bar{Z}}U_{i}\right]+\partial_{\bar{Z}}\left[\exp\left(\sum_{j}U_{j}\right)\partial_{Z}U_{i}\right]=0." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∂</mo><mi>Z</mi></msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><munder><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>j</mi></munder><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∂</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></msub><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">+</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∂</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><munder><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>j</mi></munder><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∂</mo><mi>Z</mi></msub><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial_{Z}\left[\exp\left(\sum_{j}U_{j}\right)\partial_{\bar{Z}}U_{i}\right]+\partial_{\bar{Z}}\left[\exp\left(\sum_{j}U_{j}\right)\partial_{Z}U_{i}\right]=0.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2.4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Summing this equation over <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> yields</p>
<table id="S2.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial_{Z}\partial_{\bar{Z}}\exp\left(\sum_{j}U_{j}\right)=0," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∂</mo><mi>Z</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∂</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></msub><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><munder><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>j</mi></munder><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial_{Z}\partial_{\bar{Z}}\exp\left(\sum_{j}U_{j}\right)=0,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2.5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">which has the general solution</p>
<table id="S2.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.4" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{w}=\bar{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{w}=\bar{w}</annotation></semantics></math> if <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> are complex
conjugate, but <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{w}</annotation></semantics></math> are independent real functions if
<math id="S2.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> are real coordinates. Substituting equation
<a href="#S2.E6" title="In 2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.6</span></a> into equation <a href="#S2.E4" title="In 2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a> yields</p>

<p id="S2.SS2.p3.5" class="ltx_p">The integrability condition for <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math> is</p>

<p id="S2.SS2.p3.6" class="ltx_p">It is straightforward to check that this equation is indeed satisfied
by using equations <a href="#S2.E6" title="In 2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.6</span></a> and <a href="#S2.E7" title="In 2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.7</span></a>. These equations
also ensure that the remaining Einstein equation <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{Z\bar{Z}}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{Z\bar{Z}}=0</annotation></semantics></math>
is satisfied.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The only assumptions made above were that <math id="S2.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(Z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(Z)</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S2.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{w}(\bar{Z})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{w}(\bar{Z})</annotation></semantics></math> are non-constant. The special cases when one (or
both) of these functions is constant will be dealt with in Section
<a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Special classes of solutions ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>. With this exception, it has been demonstrated that
the most general solution of the <math id="S2.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional Einstein equations that
admits <math id="S2.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-2</annotation></semantics></math> orthogonal commuting Killing vector fields takes the form
<a href="#S2.E3" title="In 2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>, where <math id="S2.SS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are solutions of <a href="#S2.E7" title="In 2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.7</span></a>
subject to the constraint <a href="#S2.E6" title="In 2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.6</span></a>, and <math id="S2.SS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> is given by equation
<a href="#S2.E10" title="In 2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.10</span></a>. The function <math id="S2.SS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math> in this equation is given by
integrating equations <a href="#S2.E11" title="In 2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.11</span></a> and <a href="#S2.E12" title="In 2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.12</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The constraint <a href="#S2.E6" title="In 2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.6</span></a> can be eliminated by using
it to express, say, <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> in terms of <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}\ldots U_{D-2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}\ldots U_{D-2}</annotation></semantics></math>. If this is done then <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> can be written</p>
<table id="S2.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\partial_{Z}w\partial_{\bar{Z}}\tilde{w}\right)-\sum_{i&gt;1}U_{i}+\gamma," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0em">∂</mo><mi>Z</mi></msub><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∂</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></msub><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munder><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\partial_{Z}w\partial_{\bar{Z}}\tilde{w}\right)-\sum_{i&gt;1}U_{i}+\gamma,</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="S2.SS2.p5.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> is given by integrating</p>
