<p id="S3.SS2.p4.11" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.SS2.p4.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> can be written in terms of <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{w}</annotation></semantics></math> to check
that equations <a href="#S2.E23" title="In 2.3 Relation to Laplace’s equation ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.23</span></a> and <a href="#S2.E24" title="In 2.3 Relation to Laplace’s equation ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.24</span></a> are obeyed.
The explicit expression will not be written out here
since it can be obtained as a special case
of more general expressions given later in this paper.
<math id="S3.SS2.p4.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is the potential of a semi-infinite rod with vanishing thickness
and mass <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/2</annotation></semantics></math> per unit length positioned
along the <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>-axis at <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\geq\mu/4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\geq\mu/4</annotation></semantics></math>. <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is the potential of an
identical rod along the <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>-axis at <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m28" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="z\leq-\mu/4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo rspace="0em">≤</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\leq-\mu/4</annotation></semantics></math>.
The function <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> is obtained from
<a href="#S3.E10" title="In 3.2 The Schwarzschild solution ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.10</span></a> and is the potential of a rod along the <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m30" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="-\mu/4\leq z\leq\mu/4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\mu/4\leq z\leq\mu/4</annotation></semantics></math> portion of the <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>-axis, again with vanishing thickness and
mass <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/2</annotation></semantics></math> per unit length. See figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 The Schwarzschild solution ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(b). Note that
the source corresponding to the time coordinate is a finite rod for both
the <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m33" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> and the <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math> Schwarzschild solutions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Black branes.</span>
For <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D&gt;5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D&gt;5</annotation></semantics></math>, the <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional Schwarzschild solution is not a
generalized Weyl solution. However, the black branes obtained by
taking products of the <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math> Schwarzschild solution with flat
space are easily seen to be Weyl solutions. The functions <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>
associated with the flat directions are all constant, and those
associated with the Schwarzschild directions can be read off from
the results of this section.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Other four-dimensional solutions</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Other physically relevant four-dimensional Weyl solutions are:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The Israel-Khan solutions</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>.
These describe finitely many collinear black holes in static
equilibrium. The forces holding them apart arise from conical deficits
in the form of struts between the black holes, or cosmic strings
extending to infinity. If the metric is written in the Weyl form
<a href="#S1.E1" title="In 1 Introduction" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1.1</span></a> then the sources for <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math> are finite rods along the
<math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>-axis. The rods have zero thickness, mass <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/2</annotation></semantics></math> per unit length,
and do not intersect. The length of each rod determines the mass
of the corresponding black hole. If one considers infinitely many such
rods of equal length and equally spaced
then one can eliminate the need for conical singularities and
obtain a solution describing an infinite line of black holes
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The C-metric</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.
The C-metric is a four-dimensional metric that describes two black
holes accelerating apart. The force for the acceleration is provided by
a conical deficit, which occurs either in the form of a strut between
the two black holes or as a cosmic string stretching off to infinity
from each hole. The Weyl form of the C-metric was obtained in
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>. The function <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math> is the potential of a
finite rod and a semi-infinite rod, which do not intersect. Both rods
lie along the <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>-axis, have zero thickness and have mass <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/2</annotation></semantics></math> per
unit length (see figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Other four-dimensional solutions ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(a) with <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}=U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>U</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}=U</annotation></semantics></math>).
The finite rod corresponds
to one of the black holes and the semi-infinite rod is responsible for
the acceleration field (the second black hole lies beyond an
acceleration horizon, so it is not apparent in the Weyl coordinates).
Adding further finite rods sources to <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>U</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U</annotation></semantics></math> results in a metric
describing multiple accelerating black holes connected by conical
deficits <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="0110258v2/sources2.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:648/313;" width="648" height="313" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Sources for (a) C-metric; (b) black ring; (c) black hole plus
KK bubble; (d) black string and KK bubble. Note that the sources for the
<math id="S3.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>’s have to add up to an infinite rod. In the classification of
Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Classification ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>, these solutions are class II.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>New solutions</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The sources for the solutions discussed in the previous section are all
rods of zero thickness and mass <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/2</annotation></semantics></math> per unit length. The rods are on
the <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>-axis and can be finite, semi-infinite or infinite. More general
sources typically give rise to naked curvature singularities on the axis
of symmetry. Hence, in attempting to find interesting new Weyl solutions
we will consider only sources of this form. The examples of the previous
section allow us to make some general observations that are useful
when analyzing a solution given its set of sources.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>General comments</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The constraint <a href="#S2.E28" title="In 2.3 Relation to Laplace’s equation ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.28</span></a> is very restrictive: It states that the
sources for the different <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>’s must add up to an infinite rod along
the <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>-axis, again with mass <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/2</annotation></semantics></math> per unit length. Assuming that only
finitely many rods are present, it follows that either one of the
<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>’s has semi-infinite rod sources which extend to <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z=\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z=\infty</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, or there is one <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> with a semi-infinite rod source which
extend to <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z=\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z=\infty</annotation></semantics></math> and another with a semi-infinite rod source which
extend to <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. All of the other <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>’s must have bounded
sources consisting of a finite number of finite rods.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">If the source for <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is bounded (i.e. involves only finitely many
finite rods) then <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> must approach a constant far from the source. It
follows that <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> must be a flat direction in the asymptotic metric. An
example of this is provided by the Schwarzschild metrics, for which the
source corresponding to the time coordinate is a finite rod, and the
time direction does indeed become flat in the asymptotic region.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Now consider the behaviour near the sources. Assume first that <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is
a time coordinate. For the <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4,5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4,5</annotation></semantics></math> Schwarzschild solutions, the source
for <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is a finite rod and the region near this source corresponds
to the event horizon of the black hole. This is also true for the
finite rod sources in the C-metric and Israel-Khan solutions. The
semi-infinite rod source of the C-metric corresponds to a horizon that
extends to asymptotic infinity – this is an acceleration horizon,
which arises because the time coordinate behaves like a boost at
asymptotic infinity. It was shown above that flat space can also be
written in a Weyl form in which the time coordinate has a semi-infinite
rod source. This source also corresponds to an acceleration horizon,
arising because the time coordinate is a boost, i.e., the Rindler time
coordinate. To summarize,</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">finite rod sources for the time
coordinate correspond to event horizons in spacetime, and semi-infinite
rod sources correspond to acceleration horizons.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">The case in which <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is a spatial coordinate can be understood by
Euclideanizing some of the metrics discussed above. For the Euclidean
Schwarzschild solution, the finite rod source corresponds to the
“bolt” where the Euclidean time direction closes off smoothly,
provided it is identified with a suitable period. A similar
interpretation holds for Euclideanized Rindler space, with the only
difference being that in the former case, the bolt is finite in extent
(it is an <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math>) whereas in the latter case it extends to
infinity (it is <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math>). These features also occur for the
other examples above. In conclusion,</p>
<ul id="S4.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">rod sources for a spatial
coordinate <math id="S4.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> correspond to “bolts”: fixed-point sets of the
orbits of <math id="S4.I2.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial/\partial x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mo rspace="0.055em">/</mo><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial/\partial x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.
If the source for <math id="S4.I2.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> extends to infinity,
then the bolt will also extend to infinity, corresponding to an axis of
rotational symmetry with <math id="S4.I2.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> acting as the azimuthal angle.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.3" class="ltx_p">In order to avoid a conical
singularity, <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> has to be periodically identified with a particular
period determined by the sources. If there is more than one source then
there will be several bolts, and the appropriate periods for <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> at
each bolt may differ. In this case, conical singularities will result.
This occurs for the C-metric and Israel-Khan solutions as well as those
of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A final fact useful when analyzing Weyl solutions immediately follows
from the above discussion. Let <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> be a spatial coordinate with a
single finite rod source. Then <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> has to be identified with a
certain period in order to avoid a conical singularity at the bolt
corresponding to the source. Moreover, <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is a flat coordinate in
the asymptotic region. It follows that <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is most naturally
interpreted as parametrizing a KK circle at infinity. If there is more
than one finite rod source then it might no longer be possible to
remove all conical singularities by identifying <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> but one would
probably still wish to minimize the number of singularities by an
appropriate identification. Hence,</p>
<ul id="S4.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">if a spatial coordinate <math id="S4.I3.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> has only finite
rod sources then it can be interpreted as a KK coordinate in the asymptotic
region.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">The rod sources, where the KK circle shrinks to zero size, appear as
singularities in the dimensionally reduced description.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Now, since at most two of the <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>’s have sources extending to
infinity, it follows that at least <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-4</annotation></semantics></math> of the <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>’s will have
bounded sources. If one of these is the time coordinate then there will
be at least <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-5</annotation></semantics></math> spatial coordinates with bounded sources so the
asymptotic metric will have at least <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-5</annotation></semantics></math> compactified flat
directions. It follows that no <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D&gt;5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D&gt;5</annotation></semantics></math> Weyl solution can be
asymptotically flat (in the global sense) if it has sources of the form
being considered here.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Classification</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A solution will be said to be of class <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> if it has <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> finite rod
sources (as well as a suitable number of infinite, or semi-infinite rod
sources).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We make no distinction between metrics related by Wick rotation, so any
of the <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> can be chosen as the time direction. The first few classes
are:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Class 0.</span> If there are no finite rod sources then the sources
must be either an infinite rod, or two semi-infinite rods (figure
<a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3.1 Flat space ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). It was
shown above that the metric is flat in both of these cases, so flat
space is the only Class <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> solution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Class I.</span> In this class, there is a single finite rod so the other
sources must be two semi-infinite rods (figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 The Schwarzschild solution ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
There are two ways that these sources can be distributed amongst the
<math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>’s. <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a).</span> <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> has a finite rod source and <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> has both
semi-infinite rod sources. The other <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are constant. This is the
four-dimensional Schwarzschild solution (times some flat directions if
<math id="S4.SS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D&gt;4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D&gt;4</annotation></semantics></math>). <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b).</span> <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> has a finite rod source, <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{3}</annotation></semantics></math> have
semi-infinite rod sources. The other <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are constant. This is the
five-dimensional Schwarzschild solution (times some flat directions if
<math id="S4.SS2.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D&gt;5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D&gt;5</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Class II.</span> The sources are two finite rods <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{3}\leq z\leq a_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{3}\leq z\leq a_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S4.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{2}\leq z\leq a_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{2}\leq z\leq a_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and two semi-infinite rods <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\geq a_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\geq a_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\leq a_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\leq a_{3}</annotation></semantics></math> (figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Other four-dimensional solutions ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). There are four ways to distribute these
sources amongst the <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>’s. Flat dimensions (corresponding to constant
<math id="S4.SS2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>) will be neglected. <span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a).</span> <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> has a semi-infinite rod
source and a finite rod source, as does <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. This gives the
four-dimensional C-metric. <span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b).</span> <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> has a finite rod source,
<math id="S4.SS2.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> has a semi-infinite rod, <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{3}</annotation></semantics></math> has a finite rod and a
semi-infinite rod. This is a new “black ring” solution that will be
discussed in section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 The black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>. <span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c).</span> <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> have the
finite rods as sources, and <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{3}</annotation></semantics></math> has both semi-infinite rods as its
sources. This is a new <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math> solution describing a superposition of a
black hole with a Kaluza-Klein bubble. <span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(d).</span> <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> have
the semi-infinite rods as sources, <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{3}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{4}</annotation></semantics></math> have the finite rods
as sources. This is a new <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=6</annotation></semantics></math> solution describing the superposition of
a black string with a Kaluza-Klein bubble. Solutions (c) and (d) will be
discussed in sections <a href="#S4.SS5" title="4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.5</span></a> and <a href="#S4.SS6" title="4.6 Superposition of a black string and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.6</span></a>
respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> class <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> solutions for <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n&gt;2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n&gt;2</annotation></semantics></math> have all been discussed
before. If <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is odd, <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=2k-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=2k-1</annotation></semantics></math>, then the solution is an Israel-Khan
solution describing <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> black holes. If <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is even, <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=2k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=2k</annotation></semantics></math> then the
solution is a generalization of the C-metric of the form discussed in
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> and describes <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> accelerating black holes on each
side of an acceleration horizon. Conical singularities are present in
both cases.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">A solution in a given class can be reduced to a solution of a lower
class by either contracting to zero size or expanding to infinity one
of its finite rods. The limits that must be taken to recover a given
solution can be easily deduced by looking at the diagrams for sources
in figures <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3.1 Flat space ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 The Schwarzschild solution ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Other four-dimensional solutions ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
For example, from fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Other four-dimensional solutions ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(a) we easily see that the
C-metric has a limit where one recovers the <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> Schwarzschild
solution, fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 The Schwarzschild solution ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(a), by taking to infinity the
leftmost endpoint of the <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> rod. Effectively, this amounts to
removing the acceleration horizon from the metric, the well-known limit
where the acceleration of the black hole is set to zero. The C-metric
also has several limits where flat (Rindler) space, figure
<a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3.1 Flat space ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, is recovered. The II(b) solution that below will be
interpreted as a black ring, fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Other four-dimensional solutions ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(b), similarly
reduces to either a <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math> black hole (fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 The Schwarzschild solution ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(b)), or a
black string obtained as the product of the <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> black hole
(fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 The Schwarzschild solution ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(a)) and a flat spatial direction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>The black ring</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> an unconventional neutral limit for the KK charged
C-metric (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> dualized to have electric charge) was taken.
The resulting metric was interpreted as describing
a pair of KK bubbles being accelerated apart by a conical singularity.
We now show that this metric has a less exotic
interpretation if one Wick rotates it to give</p>

<p id="S4.SS3.p1.3" class="ltx_p">The parameters <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> will be taken to lie in the range <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\leq\mu\leq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\leq\mu\leq 1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, the coordinate <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> in the range <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1\leq x\leq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1\leq x\leq 1</annotation></semantics></math> and
the coordinate <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> in the range <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\leq-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\leq-1</annotation></semantics></math>. This metric clearly has
three orthogonal commuting Killing vector fields so it is a Weyl
solution. Choosing <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=x^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=x^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi=x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi=x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi=x^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi=x^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, the functions
<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are given by</p>

<p id="S4.SS3.p1.4" class="ltx_p">In order to identify the sources that produce this solution it is
necessary to work with the coordinates <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r,z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r,z</annotation></semantics></math>. From equation

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\pm\sqrt{\frac{(y^{2}-1)F(y)}{(1-x^{2})F(x)}}\frac{\partial r}{\partial y}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><msqrt><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\pm\sqrt{\frac{(y^{2}-1)F(y)}{(1-x^{2})F(x)}}\frac{\partial r}{\partial y},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.7" class="ltx_p">and</p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\mp\sqrt{\frac{(1-x^{2})F(x)}{(y^{2}-1)F(y)}}\frac{\partial r}{\partial x}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>∓</mo><mrow><msqrt><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\mp\sqrt{\frac{(1-x^{2})F(x)}{(y^{2}-1)F(y)}}\frac{\partial r}{\partial x}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.9)</span></td></tr></tbody>

<p id="S4.SS3.p1.8" class="ltx_p">These equations can be integrated to give</p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.9" class="ltx_p">up to a choice of sign and an arbitrary additive constant.</p>
</div>

<p id="S4.SS3.p2.4" class="ltx_p">from which it follows that <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> is the Newtonian potential
produced by a finite rod
<math id="S4.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="-\mu/(2A)\leq z\leq\mu/(2A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\mu/(2A)\leq z\leq\mu/(2A)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is the potential produced by
a semi-infinite rod <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\geq 1/(2A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\geq 1/(2A)</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is the potential
produced by a semi-infinite rod <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="z\leq-\mu/(2A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo rspace="0em">≤</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\leq-\mu/(2A)</annotation></semantics></math> and a finite rod
<math id="S4.SS3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu/(2A)\leq z\leq 1/(2A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu/(2A)\leq z\leq 1/(2A)</annotation></semantics></math>. Note that, for <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu=1</annotation></semantics></math>, these
sources reduce to those of the five-dimensional Schwarzschild solution
and hence the metric must reduce to the metric of the Schwarzschild
solution, so the function <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math> for Schwarzschild can be read off from
the above.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Analysis of the black ring</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now explain why the name “black ring” is appropriate by examining
the global structure of this solution. To start, consider how the
general comments of section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 General comments ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a> apply to this solution.
The source for <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is a finite rod, so the time direction is expected
to be asymptotically flat and there should be a horizon present. The
coordinates <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> both have semi-infinite rod sources, so
these coordinates should be periodically identified and will have the
interpretation of azimuthal angles in the asymptotic metric.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Consider the form of the
metric as <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\rightarrow-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\rightarrow-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. The <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ty</annotation></semantics></math> part of the metric
becomes</p>
<table id="S4.E19" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<p id="S4.SS4.p2.4" class="ltx_p">The metric in brackets is just that of Rindler space with

<p id="S4.SS4.p2.6" class="ltx_p">Note that the conformal factor <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F(x)</annotation></semantics></math> is always positive for <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1\leq x\leq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1\leq x\leq 1</annotation></semantics></math>. This analysis shows that the leading order part of the <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ty</annotation></semantics></math>
metric has a non-singular horizon at <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. If one examines
the subleading order terms, one finds that these are also regular
there if the same coordinate transformation is made.
It is easy to see that the other terms of the metric can also be
smoothly extended through this surface which is therefore a regular
horizon. The near-horizon metric is</p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>

<p id="S4.SS4.p2.7" class="ltx_p">and the metric of a constant <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> slice through the horizon is</p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.25)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Consider now the <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\phi</annotation></semantics></math> part of the metric, which is conformal to</p>
<table id="S4.E26" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E26.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ds_{x\phi}^{2}=\frac{dx^{2}}{1-x^{2}}+\frac{1-x^{2}}{F(x)}d\phi^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ds_{x\phi}^{2}=\frac{dx^{2}}{1-x^{2}}+\frac{1-x^{2}}{F(x)}d\phi^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.26)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-\cos\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-\cos\theta</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\leq\theta\leq\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\leq\theta\leq\pi</annotation></semantics></math>. This
gives<span id="footnote8" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">8</span>
              
              
            If <math id="footnote8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu=1</annotation></semantics></math> then the following analysis does not apply, but it is easy
to see that the <math id="footnote8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\psi\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ψ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\psi\phi</annotation></semantics></math> part of the metric describes a round
<math id="footnote8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> of radius <math id="footnote8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2/A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2/A</annotation></semantics></math> provided one identifies <math id="footnote8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="footnote8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> with
period <math id="footnote8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\sqrt{2}\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\sqrt{2}\pi</annotation></semantics></math>. This is consistent with the above comment that
the <math id="footnote8.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu=1</annotation></semantics></math> solution is just the five-dimensional Schwarzschild
solution.</span></span></span></p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E27.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ds_{x\phi}^{2}=d\theta^{2}+\frac{\sin^{2}\theta}{1+\mu\cos\theta}d\phi^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ds_{x\phi}^{2}=d\theta^{2}+\frac{\sin^{2}\theta}{1+\mu\cos\theta}d\phi^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.27)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.3" class="ltx_p">In order for this metric to be regular at <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=0</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e. <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math>), it
is necessary to identify <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> with period <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\sqrt{1+\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\sqrt{1+\mu}</annotation></semantics></math>. For
regularity at <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=\pi</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e. <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math>), it is necessary to identify
<math id="S4.SS4.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> with period <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\sqrt{1-\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\sqrt{1-\mu}</annotation></semantics></math>. It is therefore not possible
to have regularity at both <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math>. If one demands regularity
at <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> then there is a conical singularity at <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math> with deficit
angle</p>
<table id="S4.E28" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E28.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{(x=1)}=-2\pi\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+\mu}{1-\mu}}-1\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msqrt><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mfrac></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{(x=1)}=-2\pi\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+\mu}{1-\mu}}-1\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.4" class="ltx_p">which is negative so this is really an excess angle. If one demands
regularity at <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math> then there is a conical singularity at <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> with
deficit angle</p>
<table id="S4.E29" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E29.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{(x=-1)}=2\pi\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{1-\mu}{1+\mu}}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mfrac></msqrt></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{(x=-1)}=2\pi\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{1-\mu}{1+\mu}}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
