<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.29)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.5" class="ltx_p">In both cases, the <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\phi</annotation></semantics></math> part of the metric describes a surface
that is topologically <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> with a conical singularity at one of the
poles. In the full metric, this singularity is extended in two other
spatial dimensions and hence it describes a ‘‘deficit membrane’’, the
five-dimensional analogue of a four-dimensional deficit
string<span id="footnote9" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">9</span>
              
              
            For a simpler example of a deficit membrane, consider the metric <math id="footnote9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ds^{2}=-dt^{2}+dr_{1}^{2}+r_{1}^{2}d\theta_{1}^{2}+dr_{2}^{2}+r_{2}^{2}d\theta_{2}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>θ</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ds^{2}=-dt^{2}+dr_{1}^{2}+r_{1}^{2}d\theta_{1}^{2}+dr_{2}^{2}+r_{2}^{2}d\theta_{2}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>
where <math id="footnote9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> is identified with period <math id="footnote9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="footnote9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> with
period <math id="footnote9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi-\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi-\delta</annotation></semantics></math>. The deficit membrane sits at <math id="footnote9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{2}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{2}=0</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\rightarrow-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\rightarrow-1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\psi\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ψ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\psi\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> tends to zero. To analyze
this, set <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\cosh(\xi/\sqrt{1+\mu})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mi>cosh</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ξ</mi><mo>/</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\cosh(\xi/\sqrt{1+\mu})</annotation></semantics></math>. Near <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ξ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi=0</annotation></semantics></math>, the
<math id="S4.SS4.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ψ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\psi</annotation></semantics></math> part of the metric is conformal to</p>
<table id="S4.E30" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E30.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ds_{y\psi}^{2}\approx d\xi^{2}+\frac{\xi^{2}}{1+\mu}d\psi^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ψ</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ξ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><msup><mi>ξ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ψ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ds_{y\psi}^{2}\approx d\xi^{2}+\frac{\xi^{2}}{1+\mu}d\psi^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.30)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.2" class="ltx_p">This is regular at <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ξ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi=0</annotation></semantics></math> provided <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> is identified with
period <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\psi=2\pi\sqrt{1+\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ψ</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\psi=2\pi\sqrt{1+\mu}</annotation></semantics></math>. <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-1</annotation></semantics></math> is then seen as the
origin of polar coordinates and hence <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> cannot be continued beyond
<math id="S4.SS4.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1</annotation></semantics></math>. Returning to the horizon metric <a href="#S4.E25" title="In 4.4 Analysis of the black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.25</span></a>, it is
now clear that the topology of the horizon is <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}\times S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}\times S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, which
justifies calling this solution a black ring. The circumference of the
ring varies from a maximum of <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi(1+\mu)A^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi(1+\mu)A^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> to a
minimum of <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi\sqrt{1-\mu^{2}}A^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>μ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi\sqrt{1-\mu^{2}}A^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math>. Since <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> is the
polar coordinate on the <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, it follows that <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> points away from
the ring and <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=+1</annotation></semantics></math> points into the hole in the centre of the
ring. Thus the choice of where to put the conical deficit corresponds
either to having the black ring sitting on the rim of a disc shaped
deficit membrane (with negative deficit), or to it sitting on the rim of a
disc-shaped hole in an infinitely extended deficit membrane (with
positive deficit). The area of the horizon is</p>
<table id="S4.E31" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E31.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal A}_{h}=8\pi^{2}\frac{\mu^{2}(1+\mu)}{A^{3}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒜</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>μ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\cal A}_{h}=8\pi^{2}\frac{\mu^{2}(1+\mu)}{A^{3}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.31)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.3" class="ltx_p">in the former case, and</p>
<table id="S4.E32" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E32.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\cal A}_{h}=8\pi^{2}\frac{\mu^{2}\sqrt{1-\mu^{2}}}{A^{3}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒜</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>μ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>μ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\cal A}_{h}=8\pi^{2}\frac{\mu^{2}\sqrt{1-\mu^{2}}}{A^{3}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.32)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.4" class="ltx_p">in the latter.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">It is clear from the metric that the only values of <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> that
can correspond to asymptotic infinity are <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=y=-1</annotation></semantics></math>. As these values
are approached, the metric takes the asymptotic form</p>

</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p5.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\psi}=\psi/\sqrt{1+\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>ψ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo>/</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\psi}=\psi/\sqrt{1+\mu}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\phi}=\phi/\sqrt{1+\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>/</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\phi}=\phi/\sqrt{1+\mu}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{A}=A/(1+\mu)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{A}=A/(1+\mu)</annotation></semantics></math>. The quantities
<math id="S4.SS4.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>ψ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math>, both have period <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math> if the period of
<math id="S4.SS4.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> is chosen such that the conical deficit lies at <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math>. This
metric is in fact known to be flat space. The transformation</p>
<table id="S4.E34" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E34.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi=\frac{\sqrt{y^{2}-1}}{\tilde{A}(x-y)},\qquad\eta=\frac{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{\tilde{A}(x-y)}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>ξ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msqrt><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msqrt><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi=\frac{\sqrt{y^{2}-1}}{\tilde{A}(x-y)},\qquad\eta=\frac{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{\tilde{A}(x-y)},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.34)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p5.3" class="ltx_p">takes it to the form</p>
<table id="S4.E35" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E35.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ds^{2}\sim-dt^{2}+d\xi^{2}+d\eta^{2}+\xi^{2}d\tilde{\psi}^{2}+\eta^{2}d\tilde{\phi}^{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ξ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>η</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ξ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>ψ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>η</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ds^{2}\sim-dt^{2}+d\xi^{2}+d\eta^{2}+\xi^{2}d\tilde{\psi}^{2}+\eta^{2}d\tilde{\phi}^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.35)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p5.4" class="ltx_p">which is free of conical singularities if <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>ψ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>
both have period <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, which they do if the conical deficit lies at
<math id="S4.SS4.p5.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math>. If the conical deficit lies at <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> then <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> has
a conical deficit <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>δ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> given by equation <a href="#S4.E29" title="In 4.4 Analysis of the black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.29</span></a>, so
the asymptotic metric describes a flat deficit membrane in this case.
The structure of the black ring is summarized in figure
<a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.4 Analysis of the black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>

</div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Spatial sections of the black ring metric. The
coordinate <math id="S4.F4.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> is suppressed. The surfaces of constant <math id="S4.F4.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> are
nested surfaces of topology <math id="S4.F4.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>. The coordinate <math id="S4.F4.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> is
the coordinate on <math id="S4.F4.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>. The coordinates <math id="S4.F4.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.F4.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> are,
respectively, the polar and azimuthal angles on <math id="S4.F4.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. The smallest
constant <math id="S4.F4.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> surface corresponds to the horizon, at <math id="S4.F4.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. The
surface at <math id="S4.F4.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-1</annotation></semantics></math> degenerates into an axis of rotation where the
orbits of <math id="S4.F4.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> shrink to zero. The surfaces of constant <math id="S4.F4.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> are
denoted by dotted lines. <math id="S4.F4.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> points out of the ring and <math id="S4.F4.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=+1</annotation></semantics></math>
points into the ring. The conical singularity may be chosen to lie
inside the ring or, as in the case shown, outside the ring (so that it
extends to infinity). Infinity is at <math id="S4.F4.m32" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=y=-1</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">It has been shown that the black ring has an event horizon of topology
<math id="S4.SS4.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>. Naively, one might expect such a horizon to collapse
to form a spherical black hole horizon. However, the solution has
conical singularities that prevent this from occurring. These conical
singularities describe a deficit membrane that either extends to
infinity or forms a disc inside the ring. In the latter case, the
solution is asymptotically flat. We believe this to be the first
example of an asymptotically flat solution with an event horizon of
non-spherical topology. Of course, this solution requires the presence
of a conical <span id="S4.SS4.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">excess</span> angle, which corresponds to a deficit
membrane of negative tension. This is presumably unphysical, but it
will be shown in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> that the conical singularity can be
eliminated if the ring rotates in the <math id="S4.SS4.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> direction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p7.1" class="ltx_p">If the asymptotic metric does not contain a conical singularity then
the mass of the black ring can be calculated by considering the
subleading contribution to <math id="S4.SS4.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{tt}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{tt}</annotation></semantics></math>. It is easy to show that near
<math id="S4.SS4.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=y=-1</annotation></semantics></math> this behaves as</p>
<table id="S4.E36" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E36.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{tt}\sim-\left(1-\frac{2\mu(1+\mu)}{A^{2}(\xi^{2}+\eta^{2})}+\ldots\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ξ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>η</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{tt}\sim-\left(1-\frac{2\mu(1+\mu)}{A^{2}(\xi^{2}+\eta^{2})}+\ldots\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>

</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p7.2" class="ltx_p">from which it follows (see e.g. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>) that the black ring has mass</p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>

</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p7.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS4.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> is Newton’s constant in five dimensions.
Note that when <math id="S4.SS4.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu=1</annotation></semantics></math> this gives the correct value for a
five-dimensional
Schwarzschild black hole of horizon radius <math id="S4.SS4.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2/A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2/A</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p8.1" class="ltx_p">If, on the other hand, the deficit membrane extends to infinity, the
mass of the ring can be calculated by taking as a reference background
the spacetime of a membrane (without a ring), with the result</p>
<table id="S4.E38" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E38.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=\frac{3\pi\mu\sqrt{1-\mu^{2}}}{4G_{5}A^{2}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>μ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=\frac{3\pi\mu\sqrt{1-\mu^{2}}}{4G_{5}A^{2}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.38)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p9.1" class="ltx_p">The temperature of the black ring can be obtained by Euclideanizing the
near-horizon metric: <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=-i\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=-i\tau</annotation></semantics></math>. In order to avoid a new conical
singularity at <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, it is necessary to periodically
identify <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>. From equation <a href="#S4.E21" title="In 4.4 Analysis of the black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.21</span></a>, one finds that
the temperature is</p>
<table id="S4.E39" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E39.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=\frac{A}{4\pi\mu}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=\frac{A}{4\pi\mu}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.39)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p9.2" class="ltx_p">The topology of the Euclidean solution is <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(S^{3}\times S^{2})-S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(S^{3}\times S^{2})-S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>,
where the <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is covered by the coordinates <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math>
and <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>, and the <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> by <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>. The circle removed is the
circle at <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=y=-1</annotation></semantics></math> parametrized by <math id="S4.SS4.p9.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p10.1" class="ltx_p">For either choice of the position of the deficit membrane, <math id="S4.SS4.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math> or
<math id="S4.SS4.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math>, there is a Smarr relation:</p>
<table id="S4.E40" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p11.1" class="ltx_p">Let us now assume the deficit membrane is outside the ring. The action
of the Euclidean solution can be computed similarly to
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, by subtracting the action of the deficit membrane
spacetime, and yields</p>

<p id="S4.SS4.p11.2" class="ltx_p">If we now identify the free energy as <math id="S4.SS4.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F=TI=M-TS" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F=TI=M-TS</annotation></semantics></math>, then using
<a href="#S4.E40" title="In 4.4 Analysis of the black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.40</span></a> we find that the
entropy satisfies the area law</p>
<table id="S4.E42" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E42.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S=\frac{{\cal A}_{h}}{4G_{5}}=\frac{2\pi^{2}\mu^{2}\sqrt{1-\mu^{2}}}{G_{5}A^{3}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>𝒜</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>μ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>μ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S=\frac{{\cal A}_{h}}{4G_{5}}=\frac{2\pi^{2}\mu^{2}\sqrt{1-\mu^{2}}}{G_{5}A^{3}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.42)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p12.1" class="ltx_p">It is unclear whether the black ring is a stable solution, or whether
it will become unstable for a certain range of parameter values. When
the radius of the <math id="S4.SS4.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> grows to infinity we recover a translationally
invariant black string, which is known to be unstable
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>, and this suggests that the instability might set in
already for finite but large enough radius. In that case the ring would
be unstable to rippling along the <math id="S4.SS4.p12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> direction. Given the presence
of the deficit membrane, a detailed analysis is needed to settle
the issue.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All of the metrics discussed above were already known<span id="footnote10" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">10</span>
              
              
            Although the black ring metric had not been interpreted as such.</span></span></span> rather
than discovered using the general formalism of section
<a href="#S2" title="2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. However, in this section and the following section,
new class II solutions will be constructed by following the steps
described there.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The first example is the <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math> solution that was labelled II(c) above.
It will be convenient to parametrize these sources slightly differently
from above, taking <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> to be the potential of a finite rod <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu/(2A)\leq z\leq 1/(2A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu/(2A)\leq z\leq 1/(2A)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> to be the potential of a finite rod <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="-\mu/(2A)\leq z\leq\mu/(2A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\mu/(2A)\leq z\leq\mu/(2A)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{3}</annotation></semantics></math> to be the potential of the semi-infinite
rods <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\geq 1/(2A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\geq 1/(2A)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="z\leq-\mu/(2A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo rspace="0em">≤</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\leq-\mu/(2A)</annotation></semantics></math>. The parameter <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> will be
taken in the range <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0&lt;\mu&lt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0&lt;\mu&lt;1</annotation></semantics></math> (in order to prevent the rods from
overlapping). Using the same notation as
for the black ring, this gives</p>

<p id="S4.SS5.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where the <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are arbitrary constants that reflect the freedom to
rescale the coordinates <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. This will be used to avoid any conical
singularities along the axes: according to the general comments of
Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 General comments ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>, they can all be eliminated.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Following the prescription of section
<a href="#S2" title="2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, one now computes the function <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math> by writing the
functions <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> in terms of the complex coordinate <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w=r+iz" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w=r+iz</annotation></semantics></math> and then
integrating equations <a href="#S2.E20" title="In 2.3 Relation to Laplace’s equation ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.20</span></a> and <a href="#S2.E21" title="In 2.3 Relation to Laplace’s equation ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.21</span></a>. This
calculation is performed in appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Calculating 𝜈 integrals" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>. The result
is</p>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.46)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS5.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is an arbitrary constant of integration. The quantities
<math id="S4.SS5.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\zeta_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ζ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\zeta_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Y</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math> are the same as for the black ring,
equations <a href="#S4.E12" title="In 4.3 The black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.12</span></a>, <a href="#S4.E13" title="In 4.3 The black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.13</span></a>, <a href="#S4.E14" title="In 4.3 The black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.14</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For the black ring,
the coordinate transformation <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(r,z)\rightarrow(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(r,z)\rightarrow(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math> (defined by
equations <a href="#S4.E6" title="In 4.3 The black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.6</span></a>, <a href="#S4.E10" title="In 4.3 The black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.10</span></a> with <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=A</annotation></semantics></math>) gives a form
of the metric that is easier to analyze. This suggests
performing the same coordinate transformation here.
The transformation of <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="dr^{2}+dz^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">dr^{2}+dz^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> under this change of coordinates can
be obtained from the above analysis of the black
ring. In these new coordinates, the metric takes the form</p>

<p id="S4.SS5.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where the similarity with the black ring has suggested taking <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> to
be the time direction, normalized such that <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{2}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{2}=0</annotation></semantics></math>. The square of
the Riemann tensor diverges at <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1/\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1/\mu</annotation></semantics></math>, at <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=1/\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=1/\mu</annotation></semantics></math> and at
<math id="S4.SS5.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=1</annotation></semantics></math>. This suggests taking the ranges of the coordinates
to be, again, <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1\leq x\leq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1\leq x\leq 1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\leq-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\leq-1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">This metric has an event horizon at <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>,
just as for the black ring. The orbits of <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> shrink to zero size at
<math id="S4.SS5.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math>. Regularity requires that <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> is
identified with period <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math> and</p>
<table id="S4.E48" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

</table>
<p id="S4.SS5.p5.2" class="ltx_p">The orbits of <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> shrink to zero size at both <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-1</annotation></semantics></math>. The
metric will be regular in both cases if <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is identified with
period <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math> and</p>

<p id="S4.SS5.p5.3" class="ltx_p">Having made these identifications, the above metric is complete and
non-singular and cannot be extended except through the event horizon at
<math id="S4.SS5.p5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. Note that <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> could be absorbed into <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> and
can therefore be chosen to take any convenient value. The choice</p>
<table id="S4.E50" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</table>
<p id="S4.SS5.p5.4" class="ltx_p">will be made here. Letting <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi=x^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi=x^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi=x^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi=x^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, the metric
now takes the form</p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS5.p5.5" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> both have period <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math>. The event horizon at
<math id="S4.SS5.p5.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math> has topology <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To interpret this metric, it is helpful to look first at certain
limiting cases. If <math id="S4.SS5.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu\rightarrow 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu\rightarrow 0</annotation></semantics></math> then the sources for this
solution tend to the sources for a metric consisting of a flat time
direction times the <math id="S4.SS5.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> Euclidean Schwarzschild solution. This is
the metric of a static KK bubble. If <math id="S4.SS5.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu\rightarrow 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu\rightarrow 1</annotation></semantics></math> then the
sources tend to the sources for a <math id="S4.SS5.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math> black string, with <math id="S4.SS5.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>
becoming the translation coordinate along the string (one has to
rescale <math id="S4.SS5.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> by <math id="S4.SS5.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sqrt{1-\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></msqrt><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{1-\mu}</annotation></semantics></math> before taking <math id="S4.SS5.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu\rightarrow 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu\rightarrow 1</annotation></semantics></math>). Hence this metric must somehow interpolate between a static KK
bubble and a black string.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Asymptotic infinity is at
<math id="S4.SS5.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=y=-1</annotation></semantics></math>. Near <math id="S4.SS5.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=y=-1</annotation></semantics></math>, the metric takes the form<span id="footnote11" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">11</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">11</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">11</span>
              
              
            Near <math id="footnote11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=y=-1</annotation></semantics></math> one has <math id="footnote11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-x\approx 2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-x\approx 2</annotation></semantics></math> etc, however factors of <math id="footnote11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-x</annotation></semantics></math> etc
have been retained here for purposes of comparison with the KK bubble.</span></span></span></p>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E52.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\frac{1}{\tilde{A}^{2}(x-y)^{3}}\left[\frac{(1-y)F(x)}{-1-y}dy^{2}+\frac{(1-y)^{2}F(y)}{1-x^{2}}dx^{2}\right]," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\frac{1}{\tilde{A}^{2}(x-y)^{3}}\left[\frac{(1-y)F(x)}{-1-y}dy^{2}+\frac{(1-y)^{2}F(y)}{1-x^{2}}dx^{2}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS5.p7.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS5.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{A}=A/\sqrt{1+\mu}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>/</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{A}=A/\sqrt{1+\mu}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS5.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\phi}=\sqrt{(1-\mu)/(1+\mu)}\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\phi}=\sqrt{(1-\mu)/(1+\mu)}\phi</annotation></semantics></math>. This metric is what one would obtain
from the full metric <a href="#S4.E51" title="In 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.51</span></a>
with parameters <math id="S4.SS5.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\tilde{\mu},\tilde{A})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>μ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\tilde{\mu},\tilde{A})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS5.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mu}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>μ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mu}=0</annotation></semantics></math>. It
must therefore be the metric of a static KK bubble. The periodicity of
<math id="S4.SS5.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> is inconsistent with regularity at <math id="S4.SS5.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math> but this metric
is only supposed to be an approximation to the metric
<a href="#S4.E51" title="In 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.51</span></a> near <math id="S4.SS5.p7.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=y=-1</annotation></semantics></math>. The important point is that the
static KK bubble is known to be asymptotic to <math id="S4.SS5.p7.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{1,4}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{1,4}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>,
which is the KK vacuum metric. It follows that the metric
<a href="#S4.E51" title="In 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.51</span></a> must also be asymptotic to the KK vacuum, with the
KK circle parametrized by <math id="S4.SS5.p7.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p8.1" class="ltx_p">The orbits of <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> shrink to zero size at <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> and at <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-1</annotation></semantics></math>. To
understand what this means, it is convenient to consider the KK bubble
(<math id="S4.SS5.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu=0</annotation></semantics></math>) metric and how the coordinates <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math> relate to the
Schwarzschild coordinates <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(R,\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(R,\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> in this case. This can be done
by setting <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\psi\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ψ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\psi\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> equal to<span id="footnote12" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">12</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">12</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">12</span>
              
              
            The value of <math id="footnote12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> can be
fixed by looking at the sources in the Weyl form of the metric and
comparing with the Weyl form of the Schwarzschild metric: the lengths
of the rods should match.</span></span></span> <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-2M/R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-2M/R</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\phi\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\phi\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>
equal to <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}\sin^{2}\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}\sin^{2}\theta</annotation></semantics></math>. Then <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the axis
<math id="S4.SS5.p8.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-1</annotation></semantics></math> to the axis <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=\pi</annotation></semantics></math>. The surfaces of
constant <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS5.p8.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> take the form shown on the left in figure
<a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
