<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>1. Schematic depiction of the <math id="S4.F5.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R\theta</annotation></semantics></math> plane of the KK
bubble. The throat of the
bubble (where the KK circle shrinks to zero size) is at <math id="S4.F5.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R=2M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R=2M</annotation></semantics></math>.
In the <math id="S4.F5.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math> coordinates, this corresponds to
<math id="S4.F5.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S4.F5.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. The axes <math id="S4.F5.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=0,\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=0,\pi</annotation></semantics></math> correspond to <math id="S4.F5.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math>
and <math id="S4.F5.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-1</annotation></semantics></math> respectively. Solid and dashed lines denote curves of
constant <math id="S4.F5.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.F5.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> respectively. 2. The <math id="S4.F5.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="xy" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">xy</annotation></semantics></math> plane of the metric
<a href="#S4.E51" title="In 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.51</span></a>. There is a horizon at <math id="S4.F5.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math> and the KK
circle shrinks to zero size at <math id="S4.F5.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS5.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p9.1" class="ltx_p">The metric <a href="#S4.E51" title="In 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.51</span></a> contains a horizon at <math id="S4.SS5.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. At
that point, the radius of the KK circle is finite. This leads to
the picture on the right in figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
The full geometry of the spatial sections can be visualized by
considering how the KK dimension varies. This is depicted in figure
<a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. The solution describes a black hole sitting in the
“throat” of a static KK bubble.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p10.1" class="ltx_p">In order to see that the topology of the horizon is <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, note first
that the structure of the sources around the rod for the time
coordinate <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> in figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Other four-dimensional solutions ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(c) is locally the same as
the rod structure in figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 The Schwarzschild solution ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(b) (with <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> as time).
In more detail, note that for the KK bubble, the KK circle closes off
at <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=2M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=2M</annotation></semantics></math> on a <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta\in[0,\pi]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta\in[0,\pi]</annotation></semantics></math> denote the polar
coordinate on this sphere. If the black hole is now included then its
horizon intersects the <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> at a circle (parametrized by <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math>) at,
say, <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=\theta_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=\theta_{*}</annotation></semantics></math> with the exterior region at <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\leq\theta&lt;\theta_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\leq\theta&lt;\theta_{*}</annotation></semantics></math>. As one moves out of the throat, the <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> expands, the KK
circle opens up and <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{*}</annotation></semantics></math> increases. Eventually, <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{*}</annotation></semantics></math>
reaches <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> and the horizon is no longer present. One can choose
coordinates on the horizon to be <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math>. At the
initial value of <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, the circle parametrized by <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> shrinks
to zero, and at the final value <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{*}=\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{*}=\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, the circle parametrized
by <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> shrinks to zero, from which it follows that the topology of
the horizon is <math id="S4.SS5.p10.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>

</div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Geometry of the metric <a href="#S4.E51" title="In 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.51</span></a>. This picture shows
the surfaces <math id="S4.F6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi=0</annotation></semantics></math> (upper half) and <math id="S4.F6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi=\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi=\pi</annotation></semantics></math> (lower half), which
join together smoothly at <math id="S4.F6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math>. The horizon at <math id="S4.F6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds
to a black hole sitting at the centre of the “throat” of a static
Kaluza-Klein bubble.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS5.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p11.1" class="ltx_p">If <math id="S4.SS5.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu\rightarrow 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu\rightarrow 0</annotation></semantics></math> then the black hole horizon shrinks to zero,
leaving a KK bubble. If <math id="S4.SS5.p11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu\rightarrow 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu\rightarrow 1</annotation></semantics></math> then the horizon grows
until it swallows the throat of the bubble. When this happens, the KK
direction no longer closes off, and one is left with a compactified
black string with an event horizon of topology <math id="S4.SS5.p11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p12.1" class="ltx_p">If one Euclideanizes the solution then conical singularities can be
avoided if the Euclidean time direction <math id="S4.SS5.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> is periodically
indentified with a period <math id="S4.SS5.p12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=1/T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=1/T</annotation></semantics></math>, corresponding to a
temperature</p>
<table id="S4.E53" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E53.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=\frac{A}{4\pi\sqrt{\mu}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mi>μ</mi></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=\frac{A}{4\pi\sqrt{\mu}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.53)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS5.p12.2" class="ltx_p">This instanton can probably be interpreted as describing an
instability of flat space at finite temperature in KK theory.
This is a simultaneous manifestation of two different instabilities: the
bubble nucleation instability of the KK vacuum <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>
and the black hole nucleation instability of flat space at finite
temperature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>. The
instanton might also be used to describe a decay of a compactified
black string by KK bubble nucleation. Presumably this instanton is not
allowed when fermions are included.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p13.1" class="ltx_p">It is known that the static KK bubble is classically unstable so it
seems likely that a similar instability will afflict this
solution. One might therefore wonder whether there is an analogue of
the expanding KK bubble solution (described by the Wick rotated <math id="S4.SS5.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math>
Schwarzschild solution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>)
describing a black hole sitting in the throat
of the expanding bubble. Such a solution does indeed exist, and is
obtained by a Wick rotation of the black ring solution: if one lets
<math id="S4.SS5.p13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\rightarrow-i\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\rightarrow-i\tau</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS5.p13.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi\rightarrow it" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi\rightarrow it</annotation></semantics></math> in the black ring
solution then one obtains the metric<span id="footnote13" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">13</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">13</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">13</span>
              
              
            In terms of the original
notation for figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Other four-dimensional solutions ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(b), this means that the time
coordinate is <math id="footnote13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></span></span></p>
<table id="S4.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_eqnarray ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E54.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>=</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E54.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\frac{F(x)}{F(y)}d\tau^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>τ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\frac{F(x)}{F(y)}d\tau^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.54)</span></td></tr>
<tr class="ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle+" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>+</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle+</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex6.m2" class="ltx_Math" <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS5.p13.2" class="ltx_p">The causal structure of this metric can be understood by first
examining the <math id="S4.SS5.p13.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="xt" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">xt</annotation></semantics></math> part:</p>
<table id="S4.E55" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E55.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ds^{2}=\frac{dx^{2}}{1-x^{2}}-\frac{1-x^{2}}{F(x)}dt^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ds^{2}=\frac{dx^{2}}{1-x^{2}}-\frac{1-x^{2}}{F(x)}dt^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.55)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS5.p13.3" class="ltx_p">By changing to Kruskal coordinates, it can be seen that there are
regular horizons at <math id="S4.SS5.p13.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=\pm 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=\pm 1</annotation></semantics></math> with different surface
gravities. The coordinates <math id="S4.SS5.p13.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,t)</annotation></semantics></math> can be reintroduced beyond these
horizons. Continuing beyond the horizon at <math id="S4.SS5.p13.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math>, one finds that
the square of the Riemann tensor diverges at <math id="S4.SS5.p13.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1/\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>μ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1/\mu</annotation></semantics></math>. Beyond the
horizon at <math id="S4.SS5.p13.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math>, the metric is asymptotically de Sitter.
Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> shows the Carter-Penrose diagram for this
two-dimensional metric. The causal structure is the same as
Schwarzschild-de Sitter with the horizon at <math id="S4.SS5.p13.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math> corresponding to the
black hole horizon and
the horizon at <math id="S4.SS5.p13.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> corresponding to the cosmological horizon. As
for Schwarzschild-de Sitter it appears that there are many black holes
and asymptotic regions present,
but one is free to identify these if one chooses. Doing so
clearly makes the spatial sections compact.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure">
<div id="S4.F7.1" class="ltx_block"><span id="S4.F7.pic1" class="ltx_picture" style="width:0.0pt;height:0.0pt;"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" version="1.1" width="0.00" height="0.00" overflow="visible"><g transform="translate(0,0.00) scale(1,-1)"></g></svg></span><img src="0110258v2/penrose.png" id="S4.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:399/350;" width="399" height="350" alt="Refer to caption">
</div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>1. Causal structure of the two-dimensional metric
<a href="#S4.E55" title="In 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.55</span></a>. The dotted lines denote curvature singularities,
the thick solid lines denote asymptotic infinity and the thin solid
lines denote horizons. The pattern can repeat indefinitely to the left
and right, or can be made finite by identifications.
2. Causal structure of the Wick rotated black
ring metric.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS5.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p14.1" class="ltx_p">It is easy to see that the full five-dimensional metric will also have
regular horizons at <math id="S4.SS5.p14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=\pm 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=\pm 1</annotation></semantics></math>. The horizon at <math id="S4.SS5.p14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math> has topology
<math id="S4.SS5.p14.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> and the one at <math id="S4.SS5.p14.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> has topology <math id="S4.SS5.p14.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}\times R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}\times R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (with the
<math id="S4.SS5.p14.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> direction parameterized by <math id="S4.SS5.p14.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math>). Continuing beyond the
horizon at <math id="S4.SS5.p14.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math>, there is a curvature singularity as
above. Asymptotic infinity is at <math id="S4.SS5.p14.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=y</annotation></semantics></math> and lies beyond the horizon at
<math id="S4.SS5.p14.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math>. Near infinity, the metric approaches the KK vacuum with the KK
circle parametrized by <math id="S4.SS5.p14.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>. The causal structure is illustrated in
figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.<span id="footnote14" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">14</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">14</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">14</span>
              
              
            Null infinity is presumably incomplete, as for the expanding KK bubble
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>.</span></span></span>
The interpretation of this metric is
that the horizon at <math id="S4.SS5.p14.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math> is a black hole horizon (or horizons) and
the horizon at <math id="S4.SS5.p14.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> an acceleration horizon that separates causal
curves that can fall into the black hole from those that cannot owing
to the expansion of space between them and the hole. This expansion of
space is just the expansion of the throat region of a KK bubble, which
is where the black hole is located. The asymptotic region beyond the
acceleration horizon is the region outside the bubble.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.6 </span>Superposition of a black string and KK bubble</h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We parametrize the sources for the type II(d) solution as follows.
<math id="S4.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> is the potential of a semi-infinite rod <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\geq 1/(2A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\geq 1/(2A)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is
the potential of a semi-infinite rod <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="z\leq-\mu/(2A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo rspace="0em">≤</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\leq-\mu/(2A)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is the
potential of a finite rod <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="-\mu/(2A)\leq z\leq\mu/(2A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\mu/(2A)\leq z\leq\mu/(2A)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{4}</annotation></semantics></math> is
the potential of a finite rod <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu/(2A)\leq z\leq 1/(2A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu/(2A)\leq z\leq 1/(2A)</annotation></semantics></math>. This gives</p>
<table id="S4.E56" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</table>
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where the <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are arbitrary constants. As in the previous
configuration, all conical singularities can be cancelled by an
appropriate choice of these constants and periodic identifications.</p>
</div>

<p id="S4.SS6.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is arbitrary. Once again, it proves useful to convert
from the Weyl coordinates <math id="S4.SS6.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(r,z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(r,z)</annotation></semantics></math> to the black ring coordinates
<math id="S4.SS6.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math> using equations <a href="#S4.E6" title="In 4.3 The black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.6</span></a> and <a href="#S4.E10" title="In 4.3 The black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.10</span></a> (with

<p id="S4.SS6.p2.3" class="ltx_p">The coordinate <math id="S4.SS6.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> has been chosen as the time coordinate and
normalized so that <math id="S4.SS6.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{3}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{3}=0</annotation></semantics></math>. The ranges of the coordinates will again
be taken to be <math id="S4.SS6.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1\leq x\leq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1\leq x\leq 1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS6.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\leq-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\leq-1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This metric has an event horizon at <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. The orbits of
<math id="S4.SS6.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> shrink to zero at <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math>. The metric will be regular there if
<math id="S4.SS6.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is indentified with period <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math> and</p>
<table id="S4.E62" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</table>
<p id="S4.SS6.p3.2" class="ltx_p">The orbits of <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{4}</annotation></semantics></math> shrink to zero at <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=1</annotation></semantics></math>. The metric will be
regular there if <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{4}</annotation></semantics></math> is identified with period <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math> and</p>

<p id="S4.SS6.p3.3" class="ltx_p">The orbits of <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> shrink to zero at <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-1</annotation></semantics></math>. The metric will be
regular there if <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> is identified with period <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math> and</p>
<table id="S4.E64" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.64)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS6.p3.4" class="ltx_p">The constant <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> could be absorbed into <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> and can be
conveniently chosen as</p>

<p id="S4.SS6.p3.5" class="ltx_p">The metric therefore takes the form</p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS6.p3.6" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi=x^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>χ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi=x^{4}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi=x^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi=x^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi=x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi=x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> all have period
<math id="S4.SS6.p3.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math>. This metric is complete and non-singular outside of an event
horizon at <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math> with topology <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, where the <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>
is parametrized by <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This metric can be analyzed using arguments similar to those of the
previous section. It can be
seen that the metric is asymptotic to a <math id="S4.SS6.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=6</annotation></semantics></math> static KK bubble
described by the product of a flat time direction with the <math id="S4.SS6.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math>
Euclidean Schwarzschild solution. It follows that the metric is
asymptotic to the <math id="S4.SS6.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=6</annotation></semantics></math> KK vacuum <math id="S4.SS6.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{1,4}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{1,4}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, with the <math id="S4.SS6.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>
parametrized by <math id="S4.SS6.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>χ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi</annotation></semantics></math>. Note that the <math id="S4.SS6.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> of the horizon does <span id="S4.SS6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">not</span>
wrap the KK circle: spacelike infinity and the horizon both have
topology <math id="S4.SS6.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}\times S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}\times S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> but in the former case, the <math id="S4.SS6.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> is
parametrized by <math id="S4.SS6.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>χ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi</annotation></semantics></math> and in the latter by <math id="S4.SS6.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Consider the spatial topology of the static KK bubble. The centre of the
bubble (where the KK direction collapses) has topology <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>. Moving
out of the bubble, the <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> grows and the KK direction opens up so
surfaces of constant radius from the bubble have topology
<math id="S4.SS6.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}\times S^{1}_{\chi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>χ</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}\times S^{1}_{\chi}</annotation></semantics></math>. For the above solution, this geometry is
altered by the presence of an event horizon. This event horizon
intersects the minimal <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> of the static KK bubble on a <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. To
see how this happens, introduce coordinates <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\theta,\phi,\psi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ψ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\theta,\phi,\psi)</annotation></semantics></math> on
the <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> correspond to the coordinates used
above, <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\leq\theta\leq\pi/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\leq\theta\leq\pi/2</annotation></semantics></math> and the orbits of <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>
collapse at <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=\pi/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=\pi/2</annotation></semantics></math> respectively.
For example, the round metric on <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> would take the form
<math id="S4.SS6.p5.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ds^{2}=d\theta^{2}+\sin^{2}\theta d\psi^{2}+\cos^{2}\theta d\phi^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ψ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ds^{2}=d\theta^{2}+\sin^{2}\theta d\psi^{2}+\cos^{2}\theta d\phi^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The event horizon intersects the minimal <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> at some value <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=\theta_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=\theta_{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, so this intersection has topology <math id="S4.SS6.p5.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T^{2}=S^{1}_{\psi}\times S^{1}_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>ψ</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T^{2}=S^{1}_{\psi}\times S^{1}_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>. The metric outside the event horizon is at
<math id="S4.SS6.p5.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\leq\theta&lt;\theta_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\leq\theta&lt;\theta_{*}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Moving away from the centre of the bubble, the <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> expands, the KK
circle <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}_{\chi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>χ</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}_{\chi}</annotation></semantics></math> opens up and <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{*}</annotation></semantics></math> increases. When <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{*}</annotation></semantics></math>
reaches <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi/2</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> collapses to zero size. Beyond this
point, the event horizon no longer intersects the <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>. The event
horizon can therefore be parametrized by the coordinates <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\theta_{*},\chi,\psi,\phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>χ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ψ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\theta_{*},\chi,\psi,\phi)</annotation></semantics></math>. At the initial value of <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}_{\chi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>χ</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}_{\chi}</annotation></semantics></math>
shrinks to a point and at the final value <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{*}=\pi/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{*}=\pi/2</annotation></semantics></math>,
<math id="S4.SS6.p6.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> shrinks to a point. <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>ψ</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> remains finite over the
horizon. Hence the horizon has topology <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}\times S^{1}_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>ψ</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}\times S^{1}_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math>, where
the <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is parametrized by <math id="S4.SS6.p6.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\theta_{*},\psi,\phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>ψ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\theta_{*},\psi,\phi)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In the limit <math id="S4.SS6.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu\rightarrow 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu\rightarrow 0</annotation></semantics></math>, the event horizon shrinks to nothing
and the metric reduces to the static KK bubble. As <math id="S4.SS6.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu\rightarrow 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu\rightarrow 1</annotation></semantics></math>, the event horizon grows to engulf the minimal <math id="S4.SS6.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> and hence
there is nowhere that the KK direction collapses. In this limit, the
metric reduces to a black string wrapped around the KK direction, so
the event horizon has topology <math id="S4.SS6.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}\times S^{1}_{\chi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>χ</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}\times S^{1}_{\chi}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p8.1" class="ltx_p">If the metric is Euclideanized by setting <math id="S4.SS6.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=-i\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=-i\tau</annotation></semantics></math> then conical
singularities can be avoided by identifying <math id="S4.SS6.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> with period
<math id="S4.SS6.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, corresponding to a temperature</p>
<table id="S4.E67" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E67.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=\frac{A}{4\pi\sqrt{\mu}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mi>μ</mi></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=\frac{A}{4\pi\sqrt{\mu}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4.67)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS6.p8.2" class="ltx_p">The topology of the Euclidean solution is <math id="S4.SS6.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(S^{3}\times S^{3})-T^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(S^{3}\times S^{3})-T^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>,
where one <math id="S4.SS6.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is covered by the coordinates <math id="S4.SS6.p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\tau,\psi,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ψ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\tau,\psi,y)</annotation></semantics></math>
and the other by <math id="S4.SS6.p8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\chi,\phi,x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>χ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\chi,\phi,x)</annotation></semantics></math> and the <math id="S4.SS6.p8.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T^{2}=S^{1}_{\chi}\times S^{1}_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>χ</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T^{2}=S^{1}_{\chi}\times S^{1}_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> is at <math id="S4.SS6.p8.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=y=-1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p9.1" class="ltx_p">The static KK bubble is known to be unstable, which suggests that this
new solution is probably also unstable. For the black-hole bubble
solution discussed above, it was possible to obtain the solution
describing the evolution of the instability by Wick rotating the black
ring. In the present case, however, one can argue that such a solution,
if it exists, is not a class II solution, and perhaps not even a Weyl
solution.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.7 </span>Other Wick rotations</h3>

<div id="S4.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In order to complete the discussion of these new solutions, this section
will discuss the metrics obtained by Wick rotation. Thinking about the
sources for the Weyl solutions is useful in understanding what happens
when one Wick rotates the class II solutions. For example, in the
C-metric, <math id="S4.SS7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> both have a finite rod and a semi-infinite rod
as sources. Therefore it does not matter whether <math id="S4.SS7.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S4.SS7.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is
taken to be the time coordinate. For the black ring, the sources are
qualitatively different for each <math id="S4.SS7.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and hence the choice of which
<math id="S4.SS7.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is to be the time coordinate leads to physically distinct results.
These have all been discussed already. Taking <math id="S4.SS7.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> to be the time
coordinate leads to the black ring. Taking <math id="S4.SS7.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> to be the time
coordinate leads to the solution describing a pair of KK bubbles being
accelerated apart by a conical deficit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>. Finally,
taking <math id="S4.SS7.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> to be the time coordinate leads to the solution describing
an expanding KK bubble with a black hole sitting in the throat.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the new <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math> solution, II(c) (figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Other four-dimensional solutions ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(c)), it is
clear that taking <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> as the time coordinate gives physically
equivalent choices. Above we took <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> as time, giving the static black
hole-KK bubble metric. However, taking <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> to be the time direction
leads to a new metric. This is obtained from the
metric <a href="#S4.E51" title="In 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.51</span></a> by Wick rotating <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\rightarrow-i\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\rightarrow-i\tau</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S4.SS7.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi\rightarrow it" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi\rightarrow it</annotation></semantics></math>. The resulting metric is asymptotic to <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{1,2}\times T^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{1,2}\times T^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and has
acceleration horizons at <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-1</annotation></semantics></math>. The KK directions are
parametrized by <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS7.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>. Figure <a href="#S4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 4.7 Other Wick rotations ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> shows the
geometry of the spatial sections with the KK directions suppressed.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F8" class="ltx_figure">
<div id="S4.F8.1" class="ltx_block"><span id="S4.F8.pic1" class="ltx_picture" style="width:0.0pt;height:0.0pt;"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" version="1.1" width="0.00" height="0.00" overflow="visible"><g transform="translate(0,0.00) scale(1,-1)"><g transform="translate(0,0)"><g transform="translate(0,1.33) scale(1,-1)"><foreignObject width="1.33" height="1.33" overflow="visible"><Math mode="inline" tex="x=-1" text="x = - 1" xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m1">
