                      <XMApp xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m1.1.1">
                        <XMTok meaning="equals" role="RELOP">=</XMTok>
                        <XMTok font="italic" role="UNKNOWN">x</XMTok>
                        <XMApp xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m1.1.1.3">
                          <XMTok meaning="minus" role="ADDOP">-</XMTok>
                          <XMTok meaning="1" role="NUMBER">1</XMTok>
                        </XMApp>
                      </XMApp>
                    </XMath>
                  </Math></foreignObject></g></g><g transform="translate(-41.51,166.04)"><g transform="translate(0,9.03) scale(1,-1)"><foreignObject width="29.76" height="6.91" overflow="visible"><Math mode="inline" tex="y=-1" text="y = - 1" xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m2">
                    <XMath xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m2.1">
                      <XMApp xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m2.1.1">
                        <XMTok meaning="equals" role="RELOP">=</XMTok>
                        <XMTok font="italic" role="UNKNOWN">y</XMTok>
                        <XMApp xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m2.1.1.3">
                          <XMTok meaning="minus" role="ADDOP">-</XMTok>
                          <XMTok meaning="1" role="NUMBER">1</XMTok>
                        </XMApp>
                      </XMApp>
                    </XMath>
                  </Math></foreignObject></g></g><g transform="translate(13.84,48.43)"><g transform="translate(0,6.91) scale(1,-1)"><foreignObject width="27.10" height="6.91" overflow="visible"><Math mode="inline" tex="x=1" text="x = 1" xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m3">
                    <XMath xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m3.1">
                      <XMApp xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m3.1.1">
                        <XMTok meaning="equals" role="RELOP">=</XMTok>
                        <XMTok font="italic" role="UNKNOWN">x</XMTok>
                        <XMTok meaning="1" role="NUMBER">1</XMTok>
                      </XMApp>
                    </XMath>
                  </Math></foreignObject></g></g><g transform="translate(69.19,48.43)"><g transform="translate(0,6.64) scale(1,-1)"><foreignObject width="35.47" height="4.52" overflow="visible"><Math mode="inline" tex="y=-\infty" text="y = - infinity" xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m4">
                    <XMath xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m4.1">
                      <XMApp xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m4.1.1">
                        <XMTok meaning="equals" role="RELOP">=</XMTok>
                        <XMTok font="italic" role="UNKNOWN">y</XMTok>
                        <XMApp xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.m4.1.1.3">
                          <XMTok meaning="minus" role="ADDOP">-</XMTok>
                          <XMTok meaning="infinity" name="infty" role="ID">∞</XMTok>
                        </XMApp>
                      </XMApp>
                    </XMath>
                  </Math></foreignObject></g></g><g transform="translate(304.41,6.92)"><g transform="scale(1,-1)"><text fontsize="80%" xml:id="S4.F8.pic1.5">identify</text></g></g></g></svg></span><img src="0110258v2/wick1.png" id="S4.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:499/179;" width="499" height="179" alt="Refer to caption">
</div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Spatial sections of the Wick rotated black hole-KK bubble
solution <a href="#S4.E51" title="In 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.51</span></a>. The KK coordinates <math id="S4.F8.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.F8.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> are
suppressed. The diagram on the left shows the region covered by the
coordinates <math id="S4.F8.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math>. The dotted and solid lines are curves of constant
<math id="S4.F8.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.F8.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> respectively. There are acceleration horizons at <math id="S4.F8.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S4.F8.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-1</annotation></semantics></math>. The <math id="S4.F8.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> direction closes off smoothly at <math id="S4.F8.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=+1</annotation></semantics></math> and the
<math id="S4.F8.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> circle closes off smoothly at <math id="S4.F8.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. The heavy dots denote
points where both circles close off. The diagram on the right shows how
two copies of this region may be pasted together to give a complete
geometry.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The figure on the left shows
the region covered by the coordinates <math id="S4.SS7.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math>. When the metric is
analytically continued beyond the acceleration horizon at <math id="S4.SS7.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math> it
yields a new region isometric to the first. This can then be continued
beyond the horizon at <math id="S4.SS7.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-1</annotation></semantics></math> to yield yet a new region. Therefore, there
can be infinitely many such regions. By making identifications, the
number of regions can be made finite. For example, the figure on the
right shows how to identify in order to obtain just two regions. Figure
<a href="#S4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 4.7 Other Wick rotations ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> shows the resulting spatial geometry.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F9" class="ltx_figure">

                    </XMath>
                  </Math></foreignObject></g></g></g></svg></span><img src="0110258v2/wick2.png" id="S4.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:399/238;" width="399" height="238" alt="Refer to caption">
</div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>Throat region of
the II(c) solution obtained by Wick rotation of the black hole<math id="S4.F9.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>+</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+</annotation></semantics></math>bubble
metric <a href="#S4.E51" title="In 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.51</span></a> to
<math id="S4.F9.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\to-i\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\to-i\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.F9.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi\to it" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi\to it</annotation></semantics></math>. The
<math id="S4.F9.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.F9.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> circles close off at <math id="S4.F9.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=+1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.F9.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>
respectively, denoted by dotted and solid lines. Both circles close off
at the points denoted by heavy dots. As the throat expands, the distance
between these points increases and the acceleration horizons separate
regions which can receive light signals from each point.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The solution describes an expanding KK
bubble. The KK circles collapse to zero size in different regions of the
bubble’s throat. These regions intersect in points. The acceleration
horizons separate the regions that these points can causally influence
as the throat expands. The Euclidean metric is an instanton for this
decay of the <math id="S4.SS7.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{1,2}\times T^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{1,2}\times T^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> KK vacuum.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p5.1" class="ltx_p">For the new <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=6</annotation></semantics></math> solution, II(d) (figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Other four-dimensional solutions ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(d)) there
are only two physically inequivalent choices of the time coordinate. In
the discussion in Section <a href="#S4.SS6" title="4.6 Superposition of a black string and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.6</span></a> <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> was chosen as the
time direction, giving the static black string-KK bubble metric. The
remaining possibility is to take, say, <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> to be the time coordinate.
This corresponds to the Wick rotation <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\rightarrow-i\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\rightarrow-i\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi\rightarrow it" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi\rightarrow it</annotation></semantics></math> of the metric <a href="#S4.Ex10" title="In 4.6 Superposition of a black string and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.66</span></a>. The resulting
metric is asymptotic to <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{1,3}\times T^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{1,3}\times T^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, and has an acceleration
horizon at <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=-1</annotation></semantics></math>. The KK directions are parametrized by <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>χ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S4.SS7.p5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, while <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> is an azimuthal angle at infinity. One can
continue through the acceleration horizon as described above, leading
to an identical region. This solution can be interpreted as an
expanding KK bubble. The <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>χ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> circles collapse in
different regions of the bubble’s throat. In a dimensionally reduced
picture, the KK bubble appears as a singularity of topology <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>,
with <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> the azimuthal angle.
The <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\chi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>χ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi</annotation></semantics></math> circle collapses near the poles of this sphere, and
the <math id="S4.SS7.p5.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> circle collapses on the rest of the sphere. The acceleration
horizon slices through the equator. If this metric is
Euclideanized then it gives an instanton for this decay of the
<math id="S4.SS7.p5.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{1,3}\times T^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{1,3}\times T^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> vacuum.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.8 </span>Different KK reductions</h3>

<div id="S4.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have seen in section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 General comments ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a> that if a spatial
coordinate <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> has only finite rod sources, then it is naturally
interpreted as a KK compactified direction. Above we have been
considering that points are identified along the orbits of the Killing
vector <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math>. However, when there is more than one Killing
direction with compact orbits (whether their radius is asymptotically
constant or not) it is possible to perform the identifications along
the orbits of different linear combinations of the Killing vectors. Say
that <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{j}</annotation></semantics></math> are naturally identified with periodicities <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta x^{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta x^{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, in the sense that these identifications result in
the absence of (at least some) conical singularities along the axis of
symmetry. Then it would also be possible to, instead of identifying
points along the orbits of <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math>, identify them along the orbits
of <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(i)}+{\Delta x^{j}\over\Delta x^{i}}\xi_{(j)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msup></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}+{\Delta x^{j}\over\Delta x^{i}}\xi_{(j)}</annotation></semantics></math>, with no new
singularities arising. If the bolts of <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(j)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(j)}</annotation></semantics></math>
intersect over a common fixed point, then, as shown in
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>, the circle action of this linear combination
generates a Hopf fibration of <math id="S4.SS8.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>. This change in the global
identifications obviously does not affect the local structure of the
solution, but it may result in a different interpretation of the
dimensionally reduced solution. An exhaustive study of this
construction has been performed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">When applied to the Weyl solutions, the most interesting case is that
where <math id="S4.SS8.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is a KK direction with asymptotically constant radius, and
<math id="S4.SS8.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{j}</annotation></semantics></math> is an azimuthal angle. In other words,
<math id="S4.SS8.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> has only finite rod sources,
and <math id="S4.SS8.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> has at least one semi-infinite rod source. In this case, the
twisted KK circle action is interpreted as the Hopf fibration of a
magnetic monopole. The isolated fixed point of the fibration —the
common fixed point of <math id="S4.SS8.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(i)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(i)}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS8.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(j)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(j)}</annotation></semantics></math>— appears, in the
reduced spacetime, as the (singular) source of a magnetic field.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To illustrate this with an example <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>, consider adding a
flat time direction to the <math id="S4.SS8.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> Euclidean Schwarzschild solution
(refer to section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 The Schwarzschild solution ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> and figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 The Schwarzschild solution ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(a)).
<math id="S4.SS8.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> is a KK direction, with natural periodicity <math id="S4.SS8.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8\pi M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8\pi M</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS8.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>
is an azimuthal angle of period <math id="S4.SS8.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math>. With the conventional
(untwisted) identifications this describes a static KK bubble.
However, <math id="S4.SS8.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(1)}+(1/4M)\xi_{(2)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(1)}+(1/4M)\xi_{(2)}</annotation></semantics></math> generates Hopf actions with
opposite orientations around the endpoints of the rod. Identifying
points along these orbits, these endpoints appear in the reduced
four-dimensional description as a pair of oppositely charged magnetic
monopoles. This reduced spacetime is not asymptotically flat: the
change in the identifications results also in a KK magnetic Melvin
flux tube <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>, which balances the attraction between
the monopole and the antimonopole. Since the strength of the external
magnetic flux tube and the charge of the monopoles are both determined
by the amount of twist in the reduction, they are not independent
parameters.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Proceeding this way we are led to alternative interpretations of many
of the Weyl solutions that contain KK bubbles. The <math id="S4.SS8.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math> Schwarzschild
solution was found to describe in this manner a pair of oppositely
charged magnetic monopoles accelerating away under the pull of a
magnetic flux tube <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>. Consider now the
solutions in class II(b) (refer to figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Other four-dimensional solutions ‣ 3 Weyl form of known solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(b)), with
<math id="S4.SS8.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> as the KK coordinate. Dimensionally reduce along the orbits of
<math id="S4.SS8.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(1)}+{\Delta x^{3}\over\Delta x^{1}}\xi_{(3)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(1)}+{\Delta x^{3}\over\Delta x^{1}}\xi_{(3)}</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math id="S4.SS8.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is the
timelike coordinate. The endpoints of the <math id="S4.SS8.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> rod have the
four-dimensional interpretation of a magnetic monopole and antimonopole.
<math id="S4.SS8.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> has a semi-infinite rod, so <math id="S4.SS8.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is a boost coordinate and the
pair are accelerating, but notice they do it <span id="S4.SS8.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">together</span>. By
extending the solution across the acceleration horizon, we expect to
find a similar monopole-antimonopole dipole accelerating in the opposite
direction. The dipoles accelerate under the pull of a magnetic
flux tube, and each dipole is held together by the presence of a conical
singularity running between the poles.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Now suppose we reduce along the orbits of <math id="S4.SS8.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(1)}+{\Delta x^{2}\over\Delta x^{1}}\xi_{(2)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(1)}+{\Delta x^{2}\over\Delta x^{1}}\xi_{(2)}</annotation></semantics></math>. From the sources for the time coordinate
<math id="S4.SS8.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> we infer the presence of an acceleration horizon, but also of a
black hole horizon. The vectors <math id="S4.SS8.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(1)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(1)}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS8.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(2)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(2)}</annotation></semantics></math> do not
share common fixed points: in this case the magnetic charge is not
sourced by a monopole, but by a black hole. The interpretation is in
terms of a non-extremal KK magnetic black hole moving with uniform
acceleration (and its opposite counterpart, from analytic continuation,
beyond the acceleration horizon). Since, as we explained, the charge
and the magnetic field cannot be varied independently of each other,
the solution is a only particular case of the magnetic KK Ernst
solution of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In a similar vein, the II(c) solution with identifications along
<math id="S4.SS8.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi_{(2)}+{\Delta x^{3}\over\Delta x^{2}}\xi_{(3)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ξ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi_{(2)}+{\Delta x^{3}\over\Delta x^{2}}\xi_{(3)}</annotation></semantics></math> leads to a static
configuration with a magnetic monopole and an oppositely charged
magnetic black hole. A flux tube keeps them apart in (unstable)
equilibrium. The II(d) solution, with an interpretation in terms of
<math id="S4.SS8.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> compactified KK theory, admits even more combinations, which we
shall leave to the reader to analyze.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS9" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.9 </span>Multi-black hole configurations</h3>

<div id="S4.SS9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Weyl’s construction in <math id="S4.SS9.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> easily allows for configurations with an
arbitrary number of black holes along the symmetry axis: these are the
Israel-Khan solutions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>. As is obvious from physical
considerations, the conical singularities can only be cancelled if there
are an infinite number of them (and then the masses and distances
between them are properly adjusted). With such a periodic array of black
holes, it is natural to periodically identify the <math id="S4.SS9.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>-coordinate,
which gives a solution describing a black hole localized on the KK
circle of <math id="S4.SS9.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> KK theory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS9.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS9.p2.1" class="ltx_p">It is a simple matter to describe Weyl solutions in <math id="S4.SS9.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D&gt;4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D&gt;4</annotation></semantics></math> with
several disconnected horizons. This provides the first example of a
construction of static multi-black hole solutions in higher dimensional
vacuum gravity. Here we will only sketch the properties of the
solutions as deduced from their rod structure, rather than giving the
full metrics.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="0110258v2/sourcesn.png" id="S4.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:648/287;" width="648" height="287" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Sources for (a) two-black hole configuration; (b) three-black
hole configuration; (c) infinite periodic array of black holes.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS9.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS9.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The simplest solution with two black hole horizons, each of topology
<math id="S4.SS9.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>, results from the class III sources shown in figure
<a href="#S4.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 4.9 Multi-black hole configurations ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>(a). However, due to the isolated finite rod source
for <math id="S4.SS9.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, the coordinate <math id="S4.SS9.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is asymptotically a KK circle, so this
is not an asymptotically flat solution. Instead, the configuration
describes two black holes at the north and south pole of a KK bubble:
add a second black hole to figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.5 Superposition of a black hole and KK bubble ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, sitting opposite to
the one that is already present. The distribution of the sources also
reveals that no conical singularities are needed to keep the black
holes apart. When the two black holes coalesce, the solutions does not
reduce to a single, larger, black hole but rather to a black string.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS9.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS9.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A three-black hole solution is obtained from the sources of figure
<a href="#S4.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 4.9 Multi-black hole configurations ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>(b). This solution <span id="S4.SS9.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">is</span> asymptotically flat, with
the two spatial Killing directions <math id="S4.SS9.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS9.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> becoming azimuthal
angles at infinity. It necessarily contains conical singularities.
However, the black holes cannot be described as collinear. The first and
second black holes (numbering sources from the left) lie at the north
and south pole of a topological <math id="S4.SS9.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> parameterized by <math id="S4.SS9.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS9.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>,
while the second and third black holes lie similarly on another
topological <math id="S4.SS9.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> parameterized by <math id="S4.SS9.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS9.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. So the second black
hole is collinear with each of the other two, but along different axes.
If two of the black holes coalesce, then we find a configuration of a
black hole encircled by a black ring.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS9.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS9.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Solutions with an infinite number of black hole horizons can be
obtained in several ways. The simplest possibility is shown in figure
<a href="#S4.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 4.9 Multi-black hole configurations ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>(c). It is likely that conical singularities can be
eliminated from this solution if each <math id="S4.SS9.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> has sources consisting of
rods of equal length. It is natural to periodically identify the
<math id="S4.SS9.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>-axis to obtain a solution with a single black hole localized
on a KK circle, parametrized by <math id="S4.SS9.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>, of fixed length at infinity.
The coordinates <math id="S4.SS9.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS9.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> also parametrize circles but these do
not approach a constant length at infinity so they cannot be regarded
as KK directions. Spacelike infinity has topology <math id="S4.SS9.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}_{2}\times S^{1}_{3}\times S^{1}_{z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}_{2}\times S^{1}_{3}\times S^{1}_{z}</annotation></semantics></math> rather than <math id="S4.SS9.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{2}\times S^{1}_{z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{2}\times S^{1}_{z}</annotation></semantics></math> which would be
appropriate for a description of a black hole localized on a KK
circle. It is clear that other similar configurations of infinitely many rods
will suffer from the same drawback.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS9.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS9.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Configurations with multiple concentric black rings are also possible,
but we shall stop at this point.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Concluding remarks</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have succeeded in generalizing Weyl’s class of
solutions to arbitrary dimension
by finding the general solution of the vacuum Einstein
equations in <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensions that admits <math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-2</annotation></semantics></math> orthogonal commuting
non-null Killing vector fields.
There are two classes of static Weyl solutions. The first (the “generic”
Weyl solutions) is parametrized by
<math id="S5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-3</annotation></semantics></math> independent axisymmetric harmonic functions in three dimensional
flat space. The second class (the “special” Weyl solutions),
analyzed in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B The special Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>,
is parametrized by <math id="S5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-4</annotation></semantics></math> independent harmonic functions in two
dimensional flat space. All known physically relevant solutions fall
into the first class, and these solutions were all found to have
harmonic functions produced by sources consisting of thin rods on the
<math id="S5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>-axis, with mass <math id="S5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/2</annotation></semantics></math> per unit length. A natural way of
classifying the solutions was proposed, according to the number of
finite rod sources for the harmonic functions. This classification
scheme presented three new solutions as promising candidates for
deeper study.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Perhaps the most interesting new solution is the black ring of Section
<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 The black ring ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>. This is the first example of a stationary
solution of the vacuum
Einstein equations that is asymptotically flat and has an event horizon
of non-spherical topology<span id="footnote15" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">15</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">15</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">15</span>
            
            
          A toroidal horizon in
four dimensions has been observed in numerical simulations of collapse
in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>. It is a transient phase of the collapse: the hole
in the torus closes up faster than the speed of light, thereby
preventing asymptotic observers from probing the topology of the horizon
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>.</span></span></span>. The black ring is supported against collapse by a
conical deficit singularity in the form of a disc that sits inside the
ring. This singularity might be regarded as the gravitational effect of
a thin membrane of matter, much as a deficit string can be regarded as
an idealization of a real cosmic string. The deficit for the black ring
has <span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">negative</span> deficit angle, and hence corresponds to a negative
tension source. It is not likely that it can be modelled by any
reasonable matter source, since the weak energy condition would not be
obeyed. An alternative which is perhaps physically more reasonable is to
take the conical deficit to lie outside the ring. A deficit membrane of
positive tension is then present which extends to infinity, so the
solution is no longer asymptotically flat.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">If the black ring were charged, one might envisage balancing it against
collapse (and therefore cancelling the conical singularity) by immersing
it in a background field. This is actually the situation with the
five-dimensional charged black ring solution of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>,
which is the first example of a stationary solution with spacelike infinity of
spherical topology and a regular horizon of non-spherical topology. The
horizon of the ring in that case is an extremal, degenerate one, with
vanishing horizon area. It is nevertheless completely non-singular. The
presence of the background field implies that the spacetime is not
asymptotically flat, instead it asymptotes to a fluxbrane solution. An
alternative to coupling to a background field is to set the ring into
rotation. It will be shown in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> that one can indeed
obtain a vacuum solution describing an asymptotically flat rotating
black ring<span id="footnote16" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">16</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">16</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">16</span>
            
            
          Other recent solutions where rotation plays a role
in balancing charged, ring-like or tube-like configurations, have been
given in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>.</span></span></span> that is free of conical singularities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The other new solutions contain KK bubbles in addition to black holes
or black strings. Some of them describe new decays of the KK vacua with
internal <math id="S5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S5.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>T</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. We have exhibited but a few examples of the
wide range of possibilities for solutions which are singular in the KK
reduced description but nevertheless completely regular in higher
dimensions. Just as the black ring arose from a reinterpretation of a
previously known solution, maybe the other class II (or higher)
solutions have unexpected applications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We have sketched the construction of multi-black hole configurations. In
contrast to the Israel-Khan solutions in <math id="S5.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math>, the generalized Weyl
solutions cannot describe a linear array of five-dimensional black holes
(which would have symmetry <math id="S5.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf R}\times O(3)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐑</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf R}\times O(3)</annotation></semantics></math> instead of <math id="S5.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bf R}\times O(2)^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐑</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>O</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bf R}\times O(2)^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>). Nevertheless, we have given the first examples of
static vacuum multi-black hole configurations in dimension higher than
four. Unlike the Israel-Khan solutions, some of the higher dimensional
solutions with finitely many black holes do not contain conical
singularities.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T1" class="ltx_table">

the topology of finite area horizons is described. Other
interpretations, by different Wick rotations
or KK reductions, are discussed in secs. <a href="#S4.SS7" title="4.7 Other Wick rotations ‣ 4 New solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.7</span></a> and

</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">There are several directions for extensions of the Weyl classes in this
paper. Consideration of non-orthogonal Killing vectors would lead to
non-static, stationary solutions, or solutions with twists among the
axes. However, in <math id="S5.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> there is no general solution for non-orthogonal
Killing vectors, so progress here could probably only be made in special
cases. It would also be interesting to study the addition of <math id="S5.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-form
gauge fields.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p7.1" class="ltx_p">To conclude, we have performed a systematic analysis of an infinite
class of exact solutions of vacuum gravity in dimensions higher than
four, and exhibited new solutions with qualitatively new properties.
We hope that this work helps stimulate further systematic studies on the
rich structure of exact solutions of higher-dimensional gravity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p8.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S5.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Acknowledgments</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p9" class="ltx_para">

Gary Gibbons for discussions. RE
acknowledges partial support from UPV grant 063.310-EB187/98 and CICYT
AEN99-0315. HSR was supported by PPARC.</p>
</div>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Curvature components</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Introduce a vielbein for the metric of equation <a href="#S2.E3" title="In 2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>:</p>
<table id="A1.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e^{i}=e^{U_{i}}dx^{i},\qquad e^{Z}=e^{C}dZ,\quad e^{\bar{Z}}=e^{C}d\bar{Z}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>Z</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>C</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>C</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{i}=e^{U_{i}}dx^{i},\qquad e^{Z}=e^{C}dZ,\quad e^{\bar{Z}}=e^{C}d\bar{Z}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(A.1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The summation convention is not being used for the indices <math id="A1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i.j.\ldots" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mi>j</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i.j.\ldots</annotation></semantics></math>.
The tangent space metric <math id="A1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta_{\alpha\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>η</mi><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta_{\alpha\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> is given by <math id="A1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta_{ii}=\epsilon_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta_{ii}=\epsilon_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta_{Z\bar{Z}}=\eta_{\bar{Z}Z}=1/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>η</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta_{Z\bar{Z}}=\eta_{\bar{Z}Z}=1/2</annotation></semantics></math>, with other
components vanishing. The connection 1-forms are defined by</p>
<table id="A1.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="de^{\alpha}=-\omega^{\alpha}{}_{\beta}\wedge e^{\beta}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>α</mi></msup><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>ω</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>α</mi></msup><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>β</mi></msub><mo>∧</mo><mi>e</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>β</mi></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">de^{\alpha}=-\omega^{\alpha}{}_{\beta}\wedge e^{\beta},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(A.2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">and explicit calculation gives</p>
<table id="A1.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega_{iZ}=e^{-C}\partial_{Z}U_{i}e_{i},\qquad\omega_{i\bar{Z}}=e^{-C}\partial_{\bar{Z}}U_{i}e_{i},\qquad\omega_{ij}=0," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∂</mo><mi>Z</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∂</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></msub><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ω</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega_{iZ}=e^{-C}\partial_{Z}U_{i}e_{i},\qquad\omega_{i\bar{Z}}=e^{-C}\partial_{\bar{Z}}U_{i}e_{i},\qquad\omega_{ij}=0,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(A.3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>The special Weyl solutions</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When solving the Einstein equations in Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>, a
specific assumption was made in order to deal with the <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ZZ" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ZZ</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{Z}\bar{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{Z}\bar{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> components: that the functions <math id="A2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(Z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(Z)</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="A2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{w}(\bar{Z})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{w}(\bar{Z})</annotation></semantics></math> that appear in <a href="#S2.E6" title="In 2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.6</span></a> are non-constant. In
this appendix we investigate the cases in which one or both of these
quantities is constant. Consider first the case in which <math id="A2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="A2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> are complex conjugate coordinates. Then<span id="footnote17" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">17</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">17</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">17</span>
            
            
          Note that
<math id="footnote17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(Z)^{*}\equiv\bar{w}(\bar{Z})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo>≡</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(Z)^{*}\equiv\bar{w}(\bar{Z})</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></span></span> <math id="A2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{w}(\bar{Z})=w(Z)^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{w}(\bar{Z})=w(Z)^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> so both
<math id="A2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{w}</annotation></semantics></math> must be constant. The <math id="A2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ij" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ij</annotation></semantics></math> components of the vacuum
Einstein equations therefore reduce to</p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="C(Z,\bar{Z})=-\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i}U_{i}^{2}+c(Z)+c(Z)^{*}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><msubsup><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(Z,\bar{Z})=-\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i}U_{i}^{2}+c(Z)+c(Z)^{*},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(B.7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p1.7" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c(Z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c(Z)</annotation></semantics></math> is arbitrary. This arbitrary function just reflects the
freedom to change coordinates <math id="A2.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z\rightarrow Z^{\prime}(Z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><msup><mi>Z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z\rightarrow Z^{\prime}(Z)</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus the distinct
solutions are labelled by the functions <math id="A2.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}(Z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}(Z)</annotation></semantics></math>. These <math id="A2.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-2</annotation></semantics></math> functions
are constrained by equations <a href="#A2.E4" title="In Appendix B The special Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a> and <a href="#A2.E5" title="In Appendix B The special Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a>,
so only <math id="A2.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-4</annotation></semantics></math> of them are independent. For <math id="A2.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=4</annotation></semantics></math> the solution is flat
space. For <math id="A2.p1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D&gt;4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D&gt;4</annotation></semantics></math> the solutions are non-trivial and have no
four-dimensional analogue. Note that each <math id="A2.p1.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is a solution of the
Laplace equation in two-dimensional flat space, so this special class
of solutions is determined by <math id="A2.p1.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-4</annotation></semantics></math> harmonic functions in two flat
dimensions, in contrast to the class of generic Weyl solutions
discussed in Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Solving the Einstein equations ‣ 2 Generalized Weyl solutions" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>, which was determined in terms
of <math id="A2.p1.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-3</annotation></semantics></math> axisymmetric harmonic functions in three flat dimensions.
In <math id="A2.p1.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=5</annotation></semantics></math>, it is possible to explicitly solve the constraints on the
<math id="A2.p1.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>’s to obtain a line element parametrized by an arbitrary function
of one complex coordinate.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Now consider the case in which <math id="A2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> are independent real
coordinates and <math id="A2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{w}</annotation></semantics></math> is constant but <math id="A2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(Z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(Z)</annotation></semantics></math> is not. <math id="A2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>w</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{w}</annotation></semantics></math>
can be absorbed into <math id="A2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(Z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(Z)</annotation></semantics></math>. The <math id="A2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ij" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ij</annotation></semantics></math> Einstein equations reduce to</p>
